sections.heading: 2.2 Failure Analysis: Taxonomy and Process-level Trajectory.
sections.text: Given the strong performance of coding agents, we investigate the challenges they face in omni content processing. We propose a new failure mode taxonomy based on task type, and sample 200 trajectories (6,268 steps in total) across different models and benchmarks, along with their primary failure reasons. For each trajectory, we construct a DAG to identify its main trunk and branches, enabling process-level annotation. The resulting taxonomy comprises six failure modes: (i) Audio Perception and Extraction , (ii) Video Perception and Extraction , (iii) Insufficient Exploration of Modal Content , (iv) Knowledge Retrieval and Factual , (v) Logical Reasoning and Calculation , and (vi) Tool and Environment Infrastructure . Detailed definitions and representative examples are deferred to Appendix G . To scale the analysis beyond the 200 hand-annotated trajectories, we use GPT-5.5 as the process-level judge, which we validate against human labels on this small benchmark (see Appendix 8 for the validation protocol and results). Figure 5 reports the empirical distribution of the six failure modes across four coding agents on OmniGAIA . Knowledge-Retrieval dominates the residual errors for three of four agents (Kimi 40%, Sonnet 43%, MiniMax 35%), while Codex-GPT5.4-Low is distinctive in that Tool/Environment Failure (21%) and Insufficient Exploration (20%) each rival its knowledge errors (27%). MiniMax further stands out for heavy Video-Perception errors (28%), indicating that different agents break down along different axes of the taxonomy. Beyond aggregate rates, Figure 4 dissects a single OmniGAIA trajectory as a DAG of annotated steps, showing how multiple modes from our taxonomy—audio-perception errors, rule violations, and scraping failures—co-occur with exploration-with-recovery behavior inside the same run, and how the agent ultimately recovers the correct answer. Figure 6 : A representative OmniGAIA case comparing GPT-5.4 high without Skills and with Human-in-the-loop Skills. The no-Skills run answers incorrectly by directly applying the Southern B.C. special 400 m rule to Tofino, whereas the Human-in-the-loop-Skills run answers correctly using 200 m rule for the waters immediately offshore of Tofino.

sections.heading: 2.3 Skills and Self-Evolution for Strong Many-modality Content Processing
sections.text: Experiment Setups. Following recent work, we treat Skills as structured, inference-time packages of procedural knowledge that supply reusable workflows, instructions, and optionally executable resources to an agent ( Li et al., 2026b , Xu and Yan, 2026 ) . Unless explicitly stated otherwise, the main results in this paper are reported without Skills. We study three settings as follows: • Calibration-set self-iteration. The agent is given a small calibration set and iteratively revises its Skills using only binary correctness feedback; we reveal whether an attempt is correct or incorrect, but do not provide any human-written diagnosis of the intermediate process. • Log-driven self-distillation. A separate agent reviews raw execution logs, extracts recurring success and failure patterns, and writes Skills from these traces. This setting is inspired by recent log- and trace-driven harness optimization work such as Meta-Harness ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . • Human-in-the-loop Skills. We provide manually written Skills that encode a strong human route or best-known workflow. This setting serves as an approximate upper bound on the value of explicit procedural knowledge, while also introducing human prior and route bias. Results and Analysis. Figure 7 shows that explicit Skills consistently improve OmniGAIA performance over the No Skills baseline across all difficulty levels. All skill-enhanced variants raise average accuracy, with gains remaining visible on the High split. The best setting improves average accuracy from 61.4% to 76.7%, suggesting that inference-time procedural knowledge can substantially strengthen omni-modal agent performance. Figure 6 provides a representative example, where Skills help the agent avoid an incorrect application of regional rules and reach the correct answer. Figure 7 : Performance of GPT-5.4 high on OmniGAIA under four settings. Both self-improving methods outperform the baseline, with Log-driven self-distillation achieving the strongest results: 76.7% average accuracy versus 73.0% for Calibration-set self-iteration , and the gap widens on harder problems (65.4% vs. 59.0% on the High split). Execution traces appear to provide richer supervision than binary feedback from a small calibration set, aggregating recurring success and failure patterns from broader agent behavior rather than adapting to local calibration-set patterns, likely because they offer process-level signals with broader coverage, enabling more stable and generalizable skill refinement in practice.

sections.heading: 3 Code-X : Towards Stronger Coding Agent for Omnimodal Content
sections.text: Table 3 : Statistics of OmniCoding . Figure 8 : Duration distribution. Given that closed-source coding models outperform native omni-modal models in both performance and efficiency, we ask whether such capability can be elicited through post-training and reproduced on open-source models. To this end, we propose a strong baseline on Qwen-3.5-9B and Qwen-3.6-27B, with a complete SFT-then-RL training recipe, aiming to explore this direction on open-source coding agents on omnimodal content.

sections.heading: 3.1 OmniCoding : Synthesized Omnimodal Coding Agent Trajectory Dataset
sections.text: We construct OmniCoding , a dataset of 6,035 verifiable question–answer examples paired with video, audio, or image files for multimodal terminal-tool-use agents. Each example follows a unified schema with a question, a list of acceptable ground-truth answers, media paths, and source/modality/task metadata. We draw from four complementary sources, OmniGAIA-SFT-2K ( Li et al., 2026c ) , OmniVideoBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) , AVUTBenchmark ( Yang et al., 2025b ) , and Video-MME-v2 ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , keeping only the Video-MME-v2 subset requiring audio-visual or temporal reasoning. Table 3 and Figure 8 report the per-source composition and media-duration distribution. Construction proceeds in three steps: (i) Normalization , unifying all sources into the same schema with deduplicated questions and media consolidated into a flat directory; (ii) Verifiability , regenerating open-ended questions with ground-truth lists covering common surface variants (units, abbreviations, capitalization, number formats) and converting multiple-choice into option-letter answer sets; and (iii) Cross-review , verifying answer lists and task coverage. We stratified-split the data into 4,042 SFT and 1,993 RL examples by source-task key, and use exact match against the ground-truth list (extracted from an <answer> tag) as the binary RL reward.

sections.heading: 3.2 Method and Training Infrastructure
sections.text: We train the terminal agent with supervised warm-start followed by reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. All training examples follow the schema x = ( q , ℱ , 𝒴 ) x=(q,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{Y}) , where multiple-choice tasks use option-letter answer sets and open-ended tasks are assigned curated answer sets covering common aliases, units, abbreviations, capitalization, and number formats. The agent submits its final answer inside <answer> . Supervised warm start. For examples with demonstration trajectories, we fine-tune on assistant-generated tokens only, masking terminal outputs, tool responses, and environment observations from the loss. This stage teaches the basic interaction protocol: inspect files, run commands, create intermediate artifacts, recover from tool failures, and submit answers in the required format. Reward design. We design a process-aware verifiable reward that goes beyond binary answer matching, addressing three failure patterns: (1) the agent guesses without engaging the workspace, (2) it ignores the relevant modality (e.g., answering a video question from text alone), and (3) it emits malformed, escape-attempting, or otherwise broken tool calls. For each rollout τ \tau we compute with the following components: • Three-tier base reward. base ​ ( τ ) = w correct \text{base}(\tau)=w_{\text{correct}} if gated-correct (normalized exact match against 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} , modality engaged, ≥ 1 \geq 1 tool call, no escape attempt); else w fmt + w_{\text{fmt}+} if the agent terminated cleanly via task_complete with a non-empty <answer> ; else w fmt − w_{\text{fmt}-} . The format bonus does not stack with correctness; it exists solely to keep gradient signal on tried-correctly-but-answered-wrong trajectories that would otherwise collapse the group to zero variance. • Modality penalty r mod r_{\mathrm{mod}} . A fixed negative weight w mod w_{\mathrm{mod}} is charged when the task contains video or audio but the agent invokes no tool from the corresponding universe ( ffmpeg , whisper , etc.), detected by substring matching on bash commands. • Bad-tool penalty r tool r_{\mathrm{tool}} . A weighted ratio − w tool ⋅ P bad -w_{\mathrm{tool}}\cdot P_{\text{bad}} with P bad = ( n unparseable + n disallowed + n escape + n syntax-fail ) / ( 1 + n tool ) P_{\text{bad}}=(n_{\text{unparseable}}+n_{\text{disallowed}}+n_{\text{escape}}+n_{\text{syntax-fail}})/(1+n_{\text{tool}}) aggregates malformed calls, disallowed tools, gold-answer leakage attempts, and persistent shell errors. Weight values are listed in Appendix H.1 . We further apply group-level mechanisms: (i) group advantage normalization centers rewards within each group of G G sibling rollouts; (ii) zero-variance masking drops groups where all rollouts succeed or fail; (iii) active-only baseline excludes removed samples from group statistics; and (iv) dynamic filter drops groups with ≤ 1 \leq 1 active sample or near-zero variance originated from DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . GSPO update. For each task we sample G G rollouts τ i ∼ π θ old ( ⋅ ∣ x ) \tau_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x) and compute group-normalized advantages A i = ( R i − R ¯ ) / ( σ R + ϵ A ) A_{i}=(R_{i}-\bar{R})/(\sigma_{R}+\epsilon_{A}) . Let z i = ( z i , 1 , … , z i , L i ) z_{i}=(z_{i,1},\ldots,z_{i,L_{i}}) be the model-generated tokens in τ i \tau_{i} (tool outputs masked from the loss) and c i , ℓ c_{i,\ell} the transcript prefix before z i , ℓ z_{i,\ell} . Following GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , we use a length-normalized sequence-level importance ratio and optimize the clipped objective: ρ i ​ ( θ ) = exp ⁡ ( 1 L i ​ ∑ ℓ = 1 L i [ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( z i , ℓ ∣ c i , ℓ ) − log ⁡ π θ old ​ ( z i , ℓ ∣ c i , ℓ ) ] ) , 𝒥 GSPO ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 x ​ [ 1 G ​ ∑ i = 1 G min ⁡ ( ρ i ​ ( θ ) ​ A i , clip ⁡ ( ρ i ​ ( θ ) , 1 − ϵ − , 1 + ϵ + ) ​ A i ) ] . \displaystyle\rho_{i}(\theta)=\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{i}}\big[\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{i,\ell}\mid c_{i,\ell})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(z_{i,\ell}\mid c_{i,\ell})\big]\right),\qquad\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GSPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\min\!\Big(\rho_{i}(\theta)A_{i},\,\mathrm{clip}\!\big(\rho_{i}(\theta),1-\epsilon_{-},1+\epsilon_{+}\big)A_{i}\Big)\right]. Since reward is assigned to whole trajectories, sequence-level clipping is a natural fit: one importance ratio weights all generated tokens while tool outputs stay masked. Training infrastructure. Our RL system decouples sandboxed rollout generation from policy optimization. Rollout workers run the current policy in isolated workspaces, execute terminal commands, collect trajectories, parse answers, compute reward components, and return old log-probabilities and masks; the trainer consumes these logs and applies GSPO without executing tools or touching raw media. This separation is useful because omni-modal rollouts involve non-differentiable operations, while the optimizer only needs token sequences, masks, old log-probabilities, and scalar rewards. Sandboxes are hosted on a Slurm cluster with CPU/GPU nodes and storage, the trainer runs on cloud servers, and the two are connected via a Cloudflare tunnel for trajectory collection.

sections.heading: 3.3 Experiment Setups and Results
sections.text: Agent Harness. To train OmniCoding , we build a local terminal-agent harness adapted from Terminus-KIRA ( KRAFTON AI and Ludo Robotics, 2026 ) for converting raw multimodal files into small, checkable agent operations. At each episode, the environment creates an isolated workspace with the question and staged media files. The media remains in the filesystem rather than being packed into the model context, so the agent must decide how to inspect it through audio extraction, frame sampling, OCR/ASR, metadata reading, scripting, and intermediate verification. The visible action space is deliberately compact: execute_commands runs one command in a persistent shell, image_read inspects an image as a native multimodal observation, and task_complete ends the episode. Higher-level media processing is expressed through code and command-line tools rather than benchmark-specific APIs, keeping the harness lightweight but expressive. Unlike general software-engineering harnesses ( Wang et al., 2024c , SWE-agent Team, 2025 ) , our scaffold focuses on offline multimedia processing and trajectory collection: tool calls, terminal/image observations, final answers, exit reasons, and rewards are serialized for SFT filtering, RL replay, and failure analysis. Full details are in Appendix I.1 . Baselines and Evaluation Protocol. We train Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B and compare against three baselines: (i) training-free direct MLLM inference, where the model is fed visual frames sampled at fps=1 (capped at 512) together with Whisper-large ASR transcripts; (ii) the same MLLM evaluated under our harness with direct image reading; and (iii) SFT warm-up baseline. We additionally include Codex GPT-5.4 (low) under our harness as a reference. The thinking budget is set to 4K tokens; if the model fails to produce a correctly formatted answer, we issue a multi-turn reminder to re-answer in the required format, and if reasoning is truncated, the model is allowed to continue thinking. We evaluate on the same benchmark suite as before, reporting pass@1 throughout. Experiment Results and Analysis. As shown in Table 4 , model-tool-environment finetuned models are more adaptive to harness and perform much better than baseline and even direct MLLM settings that take up to 512 images. Code-X -RL-9B shows extremely reasoning and terminal tool-use capability, achieving 15.8 on VideoZeroBench, which is almost competitive to Gemini 3.1 Pro. Table 4 : Performance of Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B under different settings on four benchmarks. For the Direct MLLM setting in the OmniGAIA benchmark, we provide models with tools following their codebase. The thinking budget is fixed at 4K tokens for all settings.

sections.heading: 4 TerminalBench-O : From Many-modality Understanding to Processing
sections.text: Figure 9 : Overview of our benchmark, illustrated with Task T01. The coding agent is required to generate a highlight clip and caption from a soccer video and a player query, and its outputs are evaluated by an LLM-based judge in terms of event accuracy, video quality, and task correctness. As many-modality understanding capabilities mature, the frontier is shifting from passive understanding to active processing : editing videos, auditing image databases, and producing spec-compliant multimodal outputs. This shift reveals a gap between native omni-models, which excel at end-to-end perception but cannot directly operate on files, and coding agents, which can decompose tasks into tool-use pipelines. Yet existing benchmarks do not evaluate this capability: omnimodal benchmarks such as OmniGAIA ( Li et al., 2026c ) and LVOmniBench ( Tao et al., 2026 ) focus on QA-based perception, while coding-agent benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench ( Merrill et al., 2026a ) and Claw-Eval ( Ye et al., 2026 ) mainly target text or text+image tasks. As shown in Table 6 , none jointly cover many-modality understanding (MMU) and many-modality processing (MMP) on real-world cases. To close this gap, we introduce TerminalBench-O , the first process-level benchmark for coding agents on omnimodal tasks, requiring agents to process realistic inputs such as long videos, multilingual documents, and noisy audio through multi-stage pipelines, and evaluating both multimodal understanding and operation capability. Design Principles. TerminalBench-O comprises 50 challenging tasks across video (38%), audio (26%), image (14%), document (4%), and cross-modal (18%) categories. Four core principles guide the design: (i) Real-world cases , where all tasks are drawn from authentic sources (Internet Archive, HuggingFace datasets, public videos) rather than synthetic constructions; (ii) Multi-dimensional grading , where each task is scored along 4–8 weighted dimensions covering accuracy, cross-document consistency, and output quality; (iii) Shortcut-resistant design , which combines closed vocabularies, cross-file ID consistency checks, decoy injection, and word limits to prevent gaming; and (iv) Process-level evaluation , which validates intermediate artifacts and reasoning chains rather than only final answers. Task Categories. Representative tasks include: Video Understanding & Processing (T01a: extract 60-90s highlights from 90-min soccer broadcast by jersey number; T03a: auto-edit 5-min final cut from 3-camera meeting footage); Audio Forensics (T107a: segment 22-min concert recording into songs with tempo/defect detection; T108a: extract rhetorical devices and thematic structure from political speech); Image Database Analysis (T13a: detect wood defects with pixel-level masks; T50a: audit mislabeled images in CIFAR-10 subset). Unlike QA benchmarks, TerminalBench-O requires agents to create multimodal outputs (edited videos, text+video interleaved reports) that satisfy strict format and consistency constraints. Table 5 : Overall accuracy and average score of different coding agents on TerminalBench-O . † \dagger Models without native vision capabilities use the image-read implemented with Qwen3.5-Flash. Evaluation Protocol. Each task defines a weighted scoring formula score = ∑ i w i ⋅ m i \text{score}=\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot m_{i} where m i m_{i} are normalized metrics (IoU, F1, accuracy, LLM-judged quality). A submission passes if score ≥ 70 \text{score}\geq 70 and all gating conditions hold: required files exist, JSON schemas validate, cross-document IDs match, and outputs comply with closed vocabularies. Gating failures result in zero score regardless of partial correctness. For open-ended outputs (summaries, captions), we use LLM judges with detailed rubrics; for temporal tasks (video segmentation, audio boundaries), we apply tolerance windows (±2s) and Hungarian matching for IoU computation. Results Analysis. As shown in Table 5 , GPT-5.5 obtains the strongest results among the evaluated settings, with high and xHigh achieving the highest average scores. MiniMax M2.7 (V) performs the worst, reaching only a 4% pass rate and an average score of 0.55. Overall, the results show that TerminalBench-O remains challenging across different model and harness configurations, especially for tasks requiring reliable long-horizon tool use. Table 6 : Comparison of TerminalBench-O with existing benchmarks. ✔ denotes full support, ◐ denotes partial or mixed support, and ✘ denotes absent support. MMU and MMP mean many-modality understanding and processing. V : video, A : audio, I : image, T : text, D : document, F : files.

sections.heading: 5 Related Works
sections.text: Omnimodal Models and Evaluation Recent multimodal foundation models have advanced from single-modality extensions to omni-modal systems that jointly process speech, audio, images, and video ( Chu et al., 2024 , Sun et al., 2024 , Xu et al., 2025 , Qwen Team, 2026 , The Gemini Team, 2026 ) . As models push toward unified vision-and-speech interaction, evaluation has correspondingly shifted from task-specific video or audio benchmarks ( Li et al., 2023 , Liu et al., 2024 , Fu et al., 2024a , Wu et al., 2024 , Li et al., 2022 ) to omni-modal suites that more explicitly target joint reasoning over visual, auditory, and textual cues, with growing attention to long videos, grounded interaction, and real-world complexity ( Li et al., 2024b , Hong et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025c , Li et al., 2026c , Radwan et al., 2026 , Tao et al., 2026 , Xie et al., 2026 ) . Yet our audit shows that many supposedly audio-visual tasks still allow strong shortcuts or rely only weakly on audio ( Kim and Seo, 2025 ) , motivating more careful benchmark construction. Multimodal Agentic Tool-Use and Sandboxed Agents. Tool use has become a central mechanism for extending LLM agents beyond their parametric knowledge ( Yao et al., 2022 , Schick et al., 2023 , Qin et al., 2023 , Patil et al., 2025 , Yao et al., 2024 , Wang et al., 2025 ) , and increasingly improves multimodal understanding via active search, code generation, and tool orchestration without retraining a monolithic model ( Hu et al., 2024 , Zhao et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025b , Zhang et al., 2024a , Zhang et al., 2025a , Tao et al., 2025b , Lin et al., 2025 , Li et al., 2026a ) . The most mature form of sandboxed agency has emerged in software engineering, where models resolve real issues inside an execution environment ( Jimenez et al., 2023 , Yang et al., 2024a , Wang et al., 2024c , Kwa et al., 2025 , Cheng et al., 2026 ) , but existing work primarily targets natively textual or computational tasks. Our work takes a step beyond: we show, for the first time, that a model can use a sandboxed terminal with self-constructed tool use to solve non-native multimodal tasks, outperforming many specialized omni models and suggesting that sandboxed agency is a general mechanism for broader many-modality problem-solving.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We study offline omnimodal understanding through the lens of sandboxed coding agents in both training-free and fine-tune settings. Across multiple benchmarks, these agents solve a surprisingly large fraction of video-audio tasks by selectively retrieving and processing evidence from raw inputs, often rivaling or surpassing native omnimodal systems. We hope this work motivates a deeper study of multimodal intelligence at the model–tool–environment interface.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations
sections.text: Our study has several limitations. First, due to computing-resource constraints, the Code-X training recipe is only validated at the 9B and 27B scales (Qwen-3.5-9B and Qwen-3.6-27B), and we have not yet characterized how the recipe scales to frontier-size open-source models. Second, due to API credit constraints, several closed-source coding agents could not be evaluated on the full benchmark suite. In particular, Claude Opus 4.6 results on VideoZeroBench and Claude Opus 4.7 results across all four benchmarks are incomplete in the current draft, which means the comparison between coding agents and native omni-modal models is somewhat uneven on the closed-source side. Third, our scope is restricted to offline omni-modal tasks, where files are staged into a workspace ahead of time; conclusions do not transfer directly to streaming or interactive settings.

sections.heading: Appendix B Broader Impacts
sections.text: Our findings establish a more compute- and token-efficient pathway for offline omni-modal understanding, showing that text+image coding agents with sandboxed tool use can match or surpass native omni-modal models on many video- and audio-centric tasks while consuming fewer tokens. This lowers the resource barrier for omni-modal applications and broadens access for researchers and users who lack dedicated omni-model APIs, while our open-sourced Code-X recipe, OmniCoding dataset, and TerminalBench-O benchmark further support reproducible research at the model–tool–environment interface. As with any tool-using agent that processes video and audio, downstream deployments should incorporate standard safeguards such as content provenance, access controls, and user consent; we note that our agents operate only on user-staged files within an isolated workspace and do not autonomously take real-world actions.

sections.heading: Appendix C Adapting Sandboxed Agents for Omni-Modal Tasks
sections.text: We represent each omni-modal task as where q q is a natural-language instruction, ℱ \mathcal{F} is a set of input files, and 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} is the set of acceptable final answers. We use an answer set rather than a single reference string so that aliases, option letters, numerical formats, and unit variants can be handled uniformly in both evaluation and reinforcement learning. A native omni-modal model solves the task by packing the files into model context: where Pack ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{Pack}(\cdot) denotes model-specific media encoding, sampling, and serialization. In this formulation, video and audio are first-class model inputs. In contrast, our sandboxed agent does not need to ingest all raw media as context. The files ℱ \mathcal{F} are staged into an isolated workspace, and the agent is given the instruction and the corresponding file paths. It then interacts with the workspace through a terminal interface: it can inspect files, invoke tools such as ffmpeg , ffprobe , OCR, or ASR systems, write and execute scripts, create intermediate artifacts, and finally submit an answer. A sandbox rollout is written as where o t o_{t} is the current observation, including command outputs and workspace feedback, and a t a_{t} is the agent’s next message or terminal action. During a rollout, raw omni-modal files may be converted into task-relevant artifacts such as transcripts, sampled frames, OCR text, timestamps, tables, crops, or executable analysis scripts. The final prediction is parsed from the trajectory: where Ans ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{Ans}(\cdot) extracts the submitted answer, e.g., the content inside an <answer> tag when this format is required. Thus the two settings differ mainly in where omni-modal processing happens: This view treats raw video, audio, images, and documents as environment state rather than mandatory model context. The agent can therefore solve omni-modal tasks by adaptively reducing raw media into compact evidence that fits the native reasoning interface of a general-purpose coding model.

sections.heading: Appendix D Discussion and Future Works
sections.text: Do non-native modalities really require native end-to-end perception? Our results suggest that non-native modalities do not always require native end-to-end perception. Even in the simplest Codex and Claude Code settings, coding agents solve a surprisingly large fraction of video-audio tasks, and on OmniGAIA they can even outperform strong native omnimodal baselines. The key is not that the base model suddenly becomes an audio-video perceiver, but that the sandbox lets it decompose raw multimedia into artifacts that match its native reasoning interface, such as transcripts, key frames, timestamps, OCR, metadata, and compact summaries. In this sense, multimodal processing becomes analogous to protocol-based software access in text-domain agents: the model delegates non-native operations to the environment and then reasons over the returned evidence. This perspective is consistent with the broader shift from static function calling to environment-mediated problem solving in tool-use and terminal-agent evaluation ( Wang et al., 2025 , Merrill et al., 2026b , Cheng et al., 2026 ) . It also resonates with recent tool-augmented perception work, where explicit visual-tool policies and tool-derived perceptual signals both improve fine-grained multimodal reasoning ( Zhou et al., 2025 , Wei et al., 2026 ) . A natural next question is therefore not only whether a model is natively omni, but which capabilities should remain externalized, which can be compiled into reusable skills, and how agents should detect and recover from imperfect tool outputs. Our failure taxonomy and process-level benchmark point in this direction, suggesting that the central bottleneck is often tool selection, verification, and repair rather than the mere absence of raw multimodal encoders. Shortcuts in current video-audio benchmarks. Are current video-audio benchmarks measuring what they claim to measure? Our findings suggest only partially. When a text+image coding agent can answer many ostensibly omnimodal tasks by selectively extracting transcripts, sparse frames, or metadata, benchmark accuracy no longer cleanly measures native end-to-end audio-video understanding. This does not make such benchmarks uninformative, but it does mean that they frequently conflate at least three capabilities: native perception, external evidence acquisition, and general knowledge-based reasoning. Our results are aligned with recent audits and diagnostic studies showing that many video or audio-visual benchmarks admit strong visual, textual, or temporal shortcuts ( Kim and Seo, 2025 , Lim et al., 2026 ) . They are also consistent with benchmark-design efforts that explicitly enforce stronger audio dependence or reduce text-based shortcut channels ( Wei et al., 2026 ) . Going forward, we believe benchmark design should standardize at least three controls: reporting text-only, text+image, and agentic baselines; auditing modality dependence with masking or filtering tests; and minimizing leakage from subtitles, transcripts, metadata, and external retrieval whenever the target claim is native multimodal understanding. Conversely, when the target is multimodal agentic competence, retrieval, tool orchestration, and evidence processing should be treated as first-class evaluation targets rather than accidental shortcuts. Making this distinction explicit would help separate backbone perception from system-level problem solving, which are both important but not interchangeable. Can the same sandbox move from understanding to generation? We believe this is the most promising next step. Once an agent can inspect raw video, audio, and documents, compress them into structured evidence, and maintain task-relevant state over long horizons, it can in principle also plan edits, retrieve assets, invoke generative models, and validate outputs in a closed loop. Early multimedia-generation and agentic video-editing systems already point in this direction, showing that multimodal agents can coordinate text, images, video, music, and external tools under explicit planning and feedback loops ( Zhang et al., 2026 , Zhao et al., 2026 ) . The next frontier is to connect that generative loop with persistent multimodal memory, so that an assistant can build private memos, recap videos, highlight reels, or even broadcast-ready drafts grounded not only in a single uploaded file but in a user’s longer-term audiovisual history ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Doing so will require stronger memory management, preference modeling, provenance tracking, and process-level verification, since generated content must remain faithful both to source media and to user intent. More broadly, this points to a different picture of future omni assistants: not a single monolithic model that passively consumes everything in one shot, but a sandboxed system that can inspect, remember, transform, and generate across modalities with the right mix of reusable skills and external tools. Under this view, offline omnimodal understanding is not the endpoint of this line of work, but the substrate for practical multimedia copilots.

sections.heading: E.1 Multimodal Models and Evaluation
sections.text: Recent progress toward omni-modal assistants reflects a shift from modality-specific perception modules to unified models that can process speech, general audio, images, and video within a single system. On the model side, audio-language systems such as Qwen2-Audio ( Chu et al., 2024 ) and video-centered models such as VideoLLaMA 2 ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) and video-SALMONN ( Sun et al., 2024 ) established strong foundations for audio-visual understanding. More recent omni-modal systems, including VITA ( Fu et al., 2024b ) , OpenOmni ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , Baichuan-Omni ( Li et al., 2024a ) , Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) , and Qwen2.5-Omni ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , move toward unified and often real-time interaction across speech and vision. These systems substantially improve the practicality of omni interaction, but they also make it harder to separate intrinsic model ability from gains due to decoding strategies, longer context, or external processing pipelines. Benchmarking has evolved in parallel. Earlier suites mainly targeted either video understanding, such as MVBench ( Li et al., 2023 ) , Video-MME ( Fu et al., 2024a ) , and MLVU ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , or audio / audio-visual understanding, such as AIR-Bench ( Yang et al., 2024c ) , MMAU ( Sakshi et al., 2024 ) , and AV-Odyssey ( Gong et al., 2024 ) . While these benchmarks advanced multimodal evaluation, many still under-represent audio, weakly couple audio with video, or emphasize short-context perception more than long-horizon multimodal reasoning. Recent work therefore moves toward explicitly omni-modal and long-form evaluation. Benchmarks such as OmniBench ( Li et al., 2024b ) , OmniEval ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) , OmniGAIA ( Li et al., 2026c ) , LVOmniBench ( Tao et al., 2026 ) , SocialOmni ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , MMOU ( Goel et al., 2026 ) , and OmniPlay ( Bie et al., 2025 ) target more realistic settings that require integrating visual, auditory, and textual evidence over longer horizons. At the same time, recent audits show that several audio-video benchmarks admit strong visual shortcuts ( Kim and Seo, 2025 ) , suggesting that progress in omni-modal evaluation depends not only on stronger models but also on shortcut-resistant benchmark design and explicit measurement of true modality dependence.

sections.heading: E.2 Agentic Tool-Use
sections.text: The literature on tool-augmented language models treats external tools as a way to expand the action space of models rather than as simple add-ons. Foundational work such as ReAct ( Yao et al., 2022 ) and Toolformer ( Schick et al., 2023 ) showed that reasoning can be interleaved with actions and that models can learn when to invoke tools. Later efforts, including Gorilla ( Patil et al., 2023 ) , ToolBench ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , ToolLLM ( Qin et al., 2023 ) , BFCL ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , and τ \tau -bench ( Yao et al., 2024 ) , scaled this paradigm to large tool collections and more interactive, stateful environments. Across these works, the central shift is from static capability elicitation to environment-mediated problem solving. Executable code has emerged as one of the most expressive forms of tool use. CodeAct ( Wang et al., 2024b ) argues that executable programs provide a general interface for acting in digital environments, allowing agents to manipulate files, call libraries, and compose multi-step behaviors more flexibly than fixed action vocabularies. In multimodal settings, Visual Sketchpad ( Hu et al., 2024 ) and MLLM-Tool ( Wang et al., 2024a ) show that models can externalize perception into sketches, programs, and structured tool calls. PyVision ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and Thyme ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) further demonstrate that models can synthesize and execute Python-based image operations on demand, blurring the boundary between model capability and environment capability. This perspective is increasingly visible in video and omni-modal reasoning. OmAgent ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) , OmniAgent ( Tao et al., 2025b ) , Agent-Omni ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , and LensWalk ( Li et al., 2026a ) all treat multimodal understanding as an active process of decomposition, search, and selective inspection rather than passive end-to-end perception. LongShOTBench ( Kurpath et al., 2025 ) explicitly evaluates tool use and iterative refinement in long-video settings. More broadly, LLM-in-Sandbox argues that rich environments can elicit capabilities not apparent in static chat settings, reinforcing the view that multimodal competence may emerge from the interaction between a strong base model and an expressive tool substrate ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Together, these works motivate viewing multimodal intelligence as a property of a model–environment system rather than of a standalone backbone.

sections.heading: E.3 Terminal Coding Agents and Benchmarks
sections.text: The most mature form of sandboxed agency has so far emerged in software engineering. SWE-bench ( Jimenez et al., 2023 ) established the canonical issue-resolution setting by grounding evaluation in real GitHub issues and executable repository states. Systems such as SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024a ) , AutoCodeRover ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) , Agentless ( Xia et al., 2024 ) , and OpenHands ( Wang et al., 2024c ) explored different agent designs for this setting, ranging from search-heavy repair to lightweight execution-driven pipelines. This line of work reframes coding as long-horizon environment interaction rather than static code generation. Benchmarks have expanded accordingly. SWE-bench Verified ( OpenAI, 2024 ) improves reliability through a filtered subset, while SWE-bench Multimodal ( Yang et al., 2024b ) extends evaluation to visually grounded software issues. Terminal-Bench ( Merrill et al., 2026b ) and LongCLI-Bench ( Feng et al., 2026 ) move beyond repository patching toward broader command-line tasks and longer-horizon CLI interaction. Other recent benchmarks, including SetupBench ( Arora et al., 2025 ) , SWE-Bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , and SEC-bench ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , further broaden evaluation to environment setup, longer-horizon issue resolution, and security workflows. The ecosystem has also expanded beyond benchmark construction into self-improvement and broader autonomy evaluation. SWE-smith ( Yang et al., 2025a ) studies scalable data generation for software engineering agents, Live-SWE-agent ( Xia et al., 2025 ) explores self-evolution during deployment, and SWE-Fuse ( Wen et al., 2026 ) uses trajectory learning to improve agent performance. Beyond software-specific tasks, RE-Bench ( Wijk et al., 2024 ) , HCAST ( Rein et al., 2025 ) , and TheAgentCompany ( Xu et al., 2024 ) evaluate agents on longer-horizon work in realistic environments. At the same time, recent meta-analyses caution that benchmark realism, contamination, and task validity remain open concerns, and that high scores do not automatically imply broader engineering competence ( Martinez and Franch, 2026 , Prathifkumar et al., 2025 ) . These critiques are especially relevant when interpreting terminal-agent performance as evidence of general agentic ability.

sections.heading: Appendix F TerminalBench-O Construction Details
sections.text: TerminalBench-0 contains 50 curated terminal tasks under a shared workspace interface, each requiring the agent to create concrete artifacts under /workspace/output rather than return a short answer. Table 7: Summary statistics for TerminalBench-O .

sections.heading: Raw data.
sections.text: We ground the suite in real-source data: public research datasets, public archives, public-domain scans, and direct-download media. The sources cover broadcast/web video, AMI and legal speech, action and egocentric video, industrial and scientific imagery, geospatial data, music stems, bioacoustics, score-audio pairs, FITS files, and historical comics. Synthetic content is reserved for controlled corruptions, decoys, overlays, and auxiliary labels needed to make evaluation precise.

sections.heading: Preprocessing.
sections.text: Each source is normalized into a stable workspace representation before task packaging. We also prepare closed vocabularies, masks, catalogs, WCS headers, timestamp maps, and source-to-fixture mappings for downstream grading.

sections.heading: Construction.
sections.text: Step 1: Candidate mining. We first select source segments whose native structure supports a realistic operation task, such as eventful video intervals, speaker turns, action clips, score-aligned music excerpts. Candidate segments are filtered for duration, visibility, signal quality, annotation availability, and non-triviality before fixture generation. Step 2: Task-specific transformation. We then impose an operation or creation objective on the selected source. Some tasks add controlled corruptions, hidden mappings, decoys, overlays, splice events, synchronization errors, or multi-source audio compositions. Others keep the media unchanged but require structured deliverables such as ledgers, catalogs, action datasets, OMR alignments, reading-order tables, or redaction reports. Step 3: Hidden reference synthesis. For each instance, we write hidden references that specify the answer geometry used by the grader. These references include event windows, speaker maps, transcripts, quote spans, crop paths, clean media, masks, stem targets, timestamp curves, object tracks and closed-vocabulary labels. They are withheld from the agent but used to score both final outputs and intermediate artifacts. Step 4: Output-surface packaging. Finally, we expose each task as a small working directory rather than a question-only prompt. The visible files may include media, manifests, closed vocabularies, policy snippets, PDFs, CSVs, point clouds, FITS files, or auxiliary metadata, and the expected outputs are ordinary files such as MP4/WAV/PNG artifacts, CSV/JSON ledgers, subtitles,plots, and reports. This format keeps the benchmark native to terminal tools, ffmpeg , OCR/ASR, numerical Python, and file-system coordination.

sections.heading: Filtering.
sections.text: We apply filtering before and after packaging. Source candidates are removed if they are too short, ambiguous, silent, weakly annotated, or trivially solvable. Packaged tasks are then checked for complete schemas, aligned hidden references, active closed vocabularies, decoy coverage, and resistance to shortcuts such as pass-through media, empty manifests, constant labels, or copied templates.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Each task uses a dedicated grader with weighted dimensions and gating conditions. Deterministic checks cover temporal IoU, event recall, closed-vocabulary accuracy, WER/CER, speaker attribution, ASR preservation, signal metrics, SSIM/PSNR, mask IoU, timestamp error, catalog matching, photometric error, geospatial overlap, table consistency, and schema validity. For naturally open-form artifacts such as memos, overlays, or semantic summaries, some graders add constrained LLM/MLLM checklist axes. The final score therefore measures process-level completion: media quality, structured intermediate artifacts, format compliance, and cross-document consistency.

sections.heading: Appendix G Failure Mode Taxonomy and Process-level Trajectory Dataset
sections.text: Figure 10 : Overview of our process-level benchmark. (a) Dataset Overview: domain distribution across the union of OmniGAIA, LVOmniBench and SocialOmniBench (200 tasks); a word cloud of the question text; the distribution of annotated logical steps per task overlaid with the agent’s actual turn count. (b) Capability Analysis: per-task counts of image / audio / video inputs; required-versus-actual tool-category coverage on the OmniGAIA subset (n=152) – “Required” is drawn from required_external_tools ∪ \cup sources , “Actual” is recovered by argument-level classification of the agent trajectory; and the distribution of primary error types on the 100 incorrect trajectories we annotate. Here we provide detailed definitions of the six failure modes introduced in the main text. • Audio Perception and Extraction Error. The agent mis-transcribes, mis-segments, or mis-attributes the audio signal itself ( e.g. , ASR errors under noise or speaker confusion), so all downstream reasoning is conditioned on content that diverges from the true recording. • Video Perception and Extraction Error. The visual stream is misread at the source via blank or off-key frame sampling, OCR mistakes, or inverted event ordering, leaving later stages with incorrect evidence. • Insufficient Exploration of Modal Content. With multimodal inputs available, the agent answers from textual cues or priors, or terminates exploration before critical evidence is verified. The failure lies in the decision to stop probing rather than in perception quality. • Knowledge Retrieval and Factual Error. Given correct perception, the agent links it to wrong external knowledge through poorly specified queries, unreliable sources, conflated entities, or fabricated facts when retrieval fails. • Logical Reasoning and Calculation Error. Evidence is largely correct, but the derivation breaks down via wrong formulas ( e.g. , planar vs. spherical distance), arithmetic mistakes, or dropped conditions in multi-step deductions. • Tool and Environment Infrastructure Failure. The agent picks the right tool but is blocked by missing dependencies, sandbox permissions, or resource limits, forcing later steps to build on corrupted intermediates. Table 8: LLMs as process-level judges on our 200-trajectory subset. To scale failure mode analysis beyond the 200 human-annotated trajectories, we benchmark off-the-shelf LLMs as process-level judges and validate the chosen judge against human labels on this annotated set. Each model replays all 200 trajectories under a unified prompt, predicting a step reward ∈ { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \in\{-1,0,+1\} for every assistant step and, on the 100 incorrect trajectories, a primary error type from our taxonomy. We follow the AgentProcessBench ( Fan et al., 2026 ) definition for process reward, with the rubric summarized below. Table 9: Step-type-specific criteria for the { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} process reward. Step reward rubric. Only assistant messages are scored; user and tool messages serve as evidence. Each assistant step is judged using only information visible up to that step (no hindsight), and the three-level label is defined as follows: • + 1 +1 (correct and effective). The step is factually correct given the available evidence and clearly advances the task, e.g., appropriate tool use, evidence-supported interpretation of a tool output, an effective decision, or an explicit correction of a prior mistake. • 0 0 (neutral or exploratory). The step is reasonable but yields limited or unclear progress, e.g., sensible exploration, tentative planning, redundant recap, or a reasonable tool attempt that fails for external reasons such as a 404, timeout, or tool limitation. • − 1 -1 (incorrect or harmful). The step is factually wrong, misreads or fabricates evidence, violates system or policy constraints, repeats a failed pattern without a meaningful strategy change, or otherwise moves the trajectory away from success. We additionally apply error propagation : once a step is labeled − 1 -1 , dependent later assistant steps remain − 1 -1 until the agent explicitly corrects the mistake or starts an independent subtask no longer relying on the bad premise. We provide our annotation interface in Figure 11 . Figure 11 : Annotation interface of our process-level dataset. Table 8 compares predictions against human labels via Step Acc. and Primary Acc. GPT-5.5 wins on both metrics; GPT-5.4 is second on step agreement; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B matches GPT-5.4 on error-type accuracy at much higher throughput; GPT-5.4-mini and DeepSeek-V4-Flash trail on step reward, indicating that smaller models are not yet adequate for fine-grained process supervision here. Based on these results, we adopt GPT-5.5 as the process-level judge for all large-scale failure mode analyses in the main paper.

sections.heading: I.1 Omni-terminal Harness
sections.text: This appendix details our terminal-agent harness, adapted from Terminus-KIRA ( KRAFTON AI and Ludo Robotics, 2026 ) and designed around a single operation: turning raw multimodal files into small, checkable evidence. Each episode begins with an isolated workspace containing the question and the staged media files. Rather than packing media into the model context, files remain on disk, and the agent must decide how to inspect them: extracting audio, sampling frames, running OCR or ASR, reading metadata, writing scripts, and verifying intermediate results before answering. The agent operates through a small action space ( execute_commands , image_read , task_complete ) and expresses higher-level media operations through code and command-line tools ( ffmpeg / ffprobe , ASR, OCR, Python, OpenCV, NumPy, and self-authored scripts) rather than benchmark-specific APIs. Beyond execution, the harness is centered on trajectory collection: every tool call, terminal observation, image observation, final answer, exit reason, and reward field is serialized so the same rollout can be reused for SFT filtering, RL replay, and failure analysis. Concretely, the harness has four properties that are important for training: • Filesystem-grounded media processing. Raw video, audio, images, and documents are workspace state. The agent learns to transform them into transcripts, key frames, OCR text, timestamps, tables, and other compact evidence. • Persistent terminal interaction. Commands run in a stateful bash session with marker-based completion, bounded observations, timeout recovery, and support for scripts written during the episode. • Replay-faithful multimodal observations. image_read inserts the actual image into the main conversation, rather than replacing it with a caption from a separate model. The saved rollout therefore matches the observation distribution used for multimodal SFT/RL. • Qwen-compatible rollout collection. The tool schema is flat, malformed tool-call blocks are conservatively recovered, and requests are routed through sticky SGLang endpoints to preserve prefix-cache locality during large parallel rollouts. Episode state. Each task starts from an isolated workspace where q q is the task instruction, W 0 W_{0} contains the staged input files, and U 0 U_{0} contains the available command-line tools and Python libraries. The model does not receive the raw video or audio stream as context. Instead, it interacts with files through the terminal. During a rollout, the workspace may accumulate derived artifacts such as extracted frames, audio clips, ASR transcripts, OCR outputs, metadata files, temporary scripts, and numerical tables. The final prediction is accepted only from the benchmark-normalized <answer>...</answer> wrapper. Tool interface. The model sees three tools. The small tool set is deliberate: the terminal is the compositional interface, and the agent decides how to combine existing utilities with code it writes during the episode. Table 11: Model-visible tools in the OmniCoding harness. Agent loop. At each step, the harness sends the current conversation and tool schema to the model. If the model calls execute_commands , the command is executed in the persistent shell and the bounded output is returned as a tool observation. If it calls image_read , the harness first records a short tool acknowledgement and then appends the image itself as a multimodal observation in the main conversation. If it calls task_complete , the harness checks whether a wrapped answer already appears in the trajectory. The loop stops on successful completion, step limit, no-tool-call exhaustion, or runtime error. Shell runtime. The shell is a persistent bash subprocess. This preserves state across turns, including the current directory, environment variables, installed packages, and files created by the agent. Command completion is detected by appending a hidden marker after each command and polling until the marker appears. Terminal observations are capped with head–tail truncation, which keeps both the beginning of long outputs and the end where errors or final answers often appear. When a command times out, the harness terminates the direct child processes while keeping the shell alive. If the shell itself dies, it is restarted and the next observation warns the model that shell-local state has been lost. Native multimodal replay. The main change from a standard terminal harness is the native image_read path. A caption-only image reader is acceptable for evaluation, but it is not acceptable for multimodal policy training: the saved trajectory would contain text produced by a separate model rather than the pixels observed during rollout. Our harness instead stores image observations as multimodal content blocks in the main conversation. For Qwen-style chat templates, these messages are folded into the provider-specific tool-response format only at send time. The saved artifact remains provider-neutral and can be replayed for SFT or RL without changing the observation sequence. Qwen serving and tool-call robustness. Open-weight models served through SGLang can emit partially malformed tool-call blocks, especially when shell commands contain quotes, heredocs, or escape characters. We therefore use a flat execute_commands schema and a conservative recovery layer. If the backend returns no structured tool call but the assistant text contains a recognizable <tool_call> block, the harness reconstructs the call only when the function name is in the declared tool list and the arguments can be parsed without inventing content. Recovered calls are marked in the trajectory, so downstream data filtering can keep or drop them explicitly. Trajectory artifacts. Each rollout stores the full message sequence, parsed tool calls, shell outputs, image-observation references, final extracted answer, exit reason, and evaluation metadata. The same artifact supports three downstream uses. First, successful trajectories can be filtered into SFT examples. Second, RL training can replay the same observation distribution seen during rollout. Third, failures can be inspected at the process level: whether the agent sampled the wrong frames, trusted a bad ASR transcript, stopped too early, chose the wrong external fact, or made a calculation error. Table 12 : Trajectory fields saved by the harness. Prompt organization. The prompt is factored into reusable pieces. A static system prompt defines the tool contract. A shared workspace prefix defines sandbox, network, and answer-format rules. Benchmark-specific prompt bodies supply the actual question, options, files, and output schema. Runtime reminders are used only when the model stops without a tool call or calls task_complete before producing a wrapped answer. The exact prompt templates are shown in Figures 18 – 23 .
