sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Reasoning traces have become a valuable form of learning signals for improving and transferring the capabilities of large language models. In particular, detailed traces can help distill reasoning behavior from stronger teacher models into weaker student models. The value of capability transfer has motivated many deployed systems with reasoning models to hide raw internal traces and expose at most summaries and answers to users. As a result, we ask whether such interface-level trace hiding prevents users from obtaining useful reasoning supervision through prompting. We study this question with Reasoning Exposure Prompting (REP), a lightweight in-context elicitation method that uses shadow-model-generated demonstrations wrapped in auxiliary code-like formats to raise user-visible reasoning traces from a victim model. Across the common reasoning dataset, different victim models, and different student model distillation, REP substantially increases similarity between exposed and REP-conditioned internal traces while preserving useful reasoning signals.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Chain-of-thought prompting has made intermediate reasoning a central technique for improving large language model (LLM) performance on a variety of tasks, including arithmetic, commonsense, symbolic, and code reasoning ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Kojima et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . As a result, reasoning traces have become valuable artifacts in a variety of ways. They can serve as supervision for transferring reasoning behavior into smaller models through rationale and chain-of-thought distillation ( Magister et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ) ; provide rich explanation traces for imitation learning from stronger models ( Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) ; offer intermediate objects for supervision and step-level verification ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) ; support interpretability by making model behavior more inspectable, while raising questions about whether generated rationales are faithful to the actual answers ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Lanham et al., 2023 ; Paul et al., 2024 ) ; and offer potential safety-monitoring signals for detecting misbehavior in reasoning models ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . The same value also makes reasoning traces sensitive. If traces improve downstream models, support verification, and reveal behavioral signals, their exposure may enable capability extraction from frontier systems. Recent reports from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI describe distillation or model-extraction attempts against frontier models, including reasoning trace coercion and pipelines beyond chain-of-thought extraction ( Anthropic, 2026d ; Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026b ) . Independent policy analysis likewise identifies API-based distillation, including answers and intermediate reasoning steps, as a pathway for training student models ( Bearman, 2026 ) . Together, these reports suggest that hidden weights are insufficient protection when user interactions can reveal useful training data. In response, many commercial deployed systems no longer expose raw reasoning traces. For instance, OpenAI discusses hidden chain-of-thought as a monitoring object rather than user-facing ( OpenAI, 2024 ) ; Gemini exposes thought summaries rather than raw thoughts ( Google, 2026b ) ; and Claude’s extended thinking provides controlled transparency into step-by-step reasoning ( Anthropic, 2026a ) . This shift in restricted-trace design motivates a basic question: We address this question with Reasoning Exposure Prompting (REP). The key intuition is that a model may refuse or fail to reveal hidden reasoning when asked directly, but still follow demonstrations in which reasoning is presented as part of the user-visible output. Given a source dataset of interest D s = { ( q i s , a i s ) } i = 1 n D^{s}=\{(q_{i}^{s},a_{i}^{s})\}_{i=1}^{n} , our goal is to elicit reasoning traces for the questions in D s D^{s} from a victim model whose raw reasoning is not exposed. To achieve this, REP constructs a prefix of question–reasoning–answer demonstrations, wraps this prefix with auxiliary transformations such as markdown fences, shell commands, and others, prepends it to target question q i s q_{i}^{s} . The victim’s user-visible response is then parsed into an exposed reasoning trace and final answer. Thus, rather than directly requesting hidden reasoning, REP creates a context in which visible reasoning is the demonstrated pattern, encouraging the model to continue that pattern on the target question. End-to-end distillation utility alone does not reveal why an exposed trace is useful. A trace may improve a student model because it faithfully reflects the victim’s reasoning, or because it provides a plausible rationale generated under a different prompt-induced behavior. To distinguish these cases, we track three traces in open-weight evaluation: r 0 r_{0} , the benign internal trace under standard prompting; r 1 r_{1} , the internal trace under REP; and r 2 r_{2} , the exposed reasoning trace under REP. These traces let us evaluate four complementary properties. Structural validity asks whether REP produces a parseable reasoning-then-answer response. Exposure fidelity asks whether r 2 r_{2} reflects the REP-conditioned internal trace r 1 r_{1} . Behavior preservation asks whether REP preserves the victim’s original reasoning behavior, reflected by consistency with r 0 r_{0} and final answer. Functional utility asks whether exposed traces provide useful signals for downstream distillation. This decomposition is necessary because comparing only r 0 r_{0} and r 2 r_{2} cannot distinguish faithful exposure from a shifted reasoning path, and distillation accuracy alone cannot determine whether the useful trace reflects the victim model’s own reasoning. Our experiments use OpenThoughts-114k as source dataset, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B as victim models, Qwen3-14B as the shadow model, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the student. We study multiple REP wrappers, cross-dataset transfer, cross-model transfer, and downstream distillation. Our best configuration, markdown-fence REP with k = 3 k=3 demonstrations, selected by trace-level fidelity metrics, achieves the strongest downstream utility. Averaged across different benchmarks, it outperforms answer-only supervision by a factor of 2.09 2.09 , summarized traces by 1.25 1.25 , and TIA-style reasoning trace inversion ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) by 1.23 1.23 , while reaching 96.7 % 96.7\% of the oracle internal-trace reference. These results suggest that REP-exposed traces are not merely stylistic imitations but carry transferable reasoning signal. Our contributions are: • We introduce REP, a lightweight prompting method for eliciting exposed reasoning traces from reasoning LLMs. • We empirically study REP across prompting formats, demonstration sources, victim models, and student distillation settings, providing a controlled evaluation of when exposed traces contain useful reasoning supervision. • We provide initial evidence that exposed traces elicited by REP can improve smaller student models, even when the victim’s internal reasoning is not available to users.

sections.heading: Reasoning trace distillation.
sections.text: Reasoning traces are useful not only at inference time but also as supervision. Prior work shows that generated rationales and chain-of-thought traces can train smaller models to reason more effectively ( Magister et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ) , support self-improvement from generated rationales ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) , and provide rich explanation traces for imitation learning from stronger models ( Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Our work is motivated by this utility: if user-visible exposed traces preserve enough reasoning signal, they may serve as useful distillation data even when raw internal traces are hidden.

sections.heading: Hidden reasoning and trace recovery.
sections.text: Many deployed reasoning systems now hide, summarize, or otherwise moderate raw reasoning traces ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Baker et al., 2025 ; Google, 2026b ; Anthropic, 2026a ) . This creates a restricted-trace setting in which the user observes the final answer, and sometimes a summary, but not the full internal reasoning process. Most closely related to our setting, TIA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) trains trace inversion models to synthesize reasoning traces from visible inputs, answers, and optional summaries. This shows that useful reasoning supervision can be reconstructed without direct access to raw traces. Our work studies a complementary question: instead of training a separate inversion model, we ask whether user prompting can induce the victim model to externalize user-visible traces, whether those traces support downstream distillation.

sections.heading: Faithfulness of reasoning traces.
sections.text: Generated reasoning is not necessarily faithful to the computation that produces the final answer. LLMs can rationalize biased or incorrect answers without revealing the true factors driving the prediction ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) , and that interventions on chain-of-thought do not always causally affect final answers in a reliable way ( Lanham et al., 2023 ; Paul et al., 2024 ) . More recently, Chen et al. (2025) show that state-of-the-art reasoning models often fail to verbalize cues or hints that influence their answers. These findings are especially important for our setting: an exposed trace may look coherent and useful, but still fail to correspond to the model’s actual reasoning behavior. We therefore do not treat exposed traces as ground truth merely because they are fluent. Instead, our evaluation separates structural validity, exposure fidelity between r 1 r_{1} and r 2 r_{2} , behavior preservation relative to r 0 r_{0} , and downstream functional utility.

sections.heading: Reasoning trace leakage and mitigation.
sections.text: A related line of work studies how chain-of-thought traces can leak sensitive content. For example, CoT may leak personally identifiable information even when the final answer is sanitized, motivating defenses based on privacy-aware reasoning, inference-time filtering, or activation steering toward leakage-free thoughts ( Das et al., 2026 ; Ahrend et al., 2026 ; Batra et al., 2025 ) . Security work on prompt injection and context leakage similarly treats hidden model context as an exposure surface ( Gehlot, 2025 ) , but our study object is reasoning trace exposure rather than system-prompt or context-state extraction. Our focus is whether prompting can elicit capability-bearing traces from a model with hidden raw reasoning by design, and whether those exposed traces are faithful enough to support downstream distillation.

sections.heading: Application scenario.
sections.text: We study reasoning trace exposure in deployed reasoning models. A service provider hosts a victim model M v M_{v} whose raw internal reasoning is hidden (protected by defensive system prompt and assumed redacted from the user’s view) , exposing only the user-facing response. Raw traces are treated as sensitive artifacts: they can aid performance, monitoring, and debugging, but extracted at scale may enable capability transfer. We ask whether a black-box user can nevertheless induce useful reasoning traces through prompting alone.

sections.heading: Protected asset.
sections.text: The protected asset is the victim model’s hidden reasoning behavior on a source dataset where q j s q_{j}^{s} is a question and a j s a_{j}^{s} its final answer. The attacker initially observes no victim reasoning traces for these questions. Their goal is to obtain user-visible traces that reflect the victim’s reasoning behavior on D s D^{s} .

sections.heading: Attacker capabilities.
sections.text: The attacker has black-box prompt access to the victim model M v M_{v} : they may submit chosen prompts and observe only the resulting user-visible text. They do not observe the victim’s hidden reasoning trace, weights, logits, training data, or system prompt. The attacker may also use a shadow model M s M_{s} and an auxiliary demonstration dataset solely to construct in-context demonstrations. Crucially, D demo D^{\mathrm{demo}} is distinct from the protected traces over D s D^{s} : it provides prompting examples, not the victim traces the attacker seeks to expose.

sections.heading: Trace Observation.
sections.text: In realistic deployment, the attacker observes only the user-visible response of M v M_{v} . For controlled open-weight evaluation, we additionally record internal traces from M v M_{v} in order to quantify whether an exposed trace reflects the victim’s own reasoning behavior rather than a fabricated rationale. For each target question q j s q_{j}^{s} , we distinguish three traces: • r 0 r_{0} : the benign internal reasoning trace produced by M v M_{v} under standard prompting. • r 1 r_{1} : the internal reasoning trace produced by M v M_{v} under REP. • r 2 r_{2} : the exposed reasoning trace visible to the user under REP. We use the term internal reasoning trace as an operational object in controlled open-weight evaluation, not as a claim of a unique ground-truth cognitive process ( Anthropic, 2026c ) .

sections.heading: Attacker goals.
sections.text: The attacker’s objective is capability extraction through reasoning trace exposure: given black-box access to M v M_{v} and a source dataset D s D^{s} , they seek user-visible traces r 2 r_{2} for questions q j s ∈ D s q_{j}^{s}\in D^{s} that can train a student model M stu M_{\mathrm{stu}} . Since downstream utility alone does not show whether a trace reflects the victim’s own reasoning, we evaluate exposure using four criteria: structural validity for parseability, exposure fidelity between r 2 r_{2} and r 1 r_{1} , behavior preservation with respect to r 0 r_{0} and final-answer, and functional utility for downstream distillation. Together, these criteria distinguish reasoning exposure from faithful reasoning or prompt-induced reasoning drift.

sections.heading: 4 Reasoning Exposure Prompting
sections.text: Figure 1: Overview of REP. REP constructs k k -shot reasoning demonstrations S k S_{k} from an auxiliary dataset D demo D^{\mathrm{demo}} , transforms them with a wrapper T ⁡ ( ⋅ ) T(\cdot) , and prepends the resulting demonstrations to each target question q ∈ D s q\in D^{s} . The victim model M v M_{v} is then prompted to produce user-visible exposed reasoning r 2 r_{2} and final answer a a .

sections.text: Figure 1 illustrates the REP pipeline. We first sample k k questions from the auxiliary demonstration dataset D demo D^{\mathrm{demo}} . The design is motivated by the hypothesis that execution-like formats can make the model treat the context as text to be reproduced or inspected, rather than as ordinary natural-language reasoning. We analyze this hypothesis in Section 7 . The wrapper details are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4.4 Reasoning Trace Fidelity
sections.text: We evaluate reasoning exposure along four dimensions: structural validity, exposure fidelity, behavior preservation, and functional utility.

sections.heading: Structural validity.
sections.text: We report Struct%, the percentage of responses that can be parsed into the expected reasoning-then-answer format, e.g., valid <think> and <answer> blocks.

sections.heading: Exposure fidelity.
sections.text: We measure whether the exposed trace reflects the victim’s REP-conditioned internal reasoning by reporting ROUGE − L ⁡ ( r 1 , r 2 ) \mathrm{ROUGE-L}(r_{1},r_{2}) . Higher overlap indicates that the user-visible trace more closely resembles the victim’s internal reasoning under the same REP prompt.

sections.heading: Behavior preservation.
sections.text: A faithful exposed trace is meaningful only if REP does not substantially change the victim’s task behavior. We therefore compare standard and REP-conditioned runs using answer match and R 01 R_{01} , where R 01 = ROUGE − L ⁡ ( r 0 , r 1 ) R_{01}=\mathrm{ROUGE-L}(r_{0},r_{1}) . We also report R 02 = ROUGE − L ⁡ ( r 0 , r 2 ) R_{02}=\mathrm{ROUGE-L}(r_{0},r_{2}) to check whether the visible trace remains aligned with the benign reasoning path.

sections.heading: Functional utility.
sections.text: Finally, we test whether exposed traces provide useful supervision for downstream distillation. We fine-tune a student model M stu M_{\mathrm{stu}} on and evaluate the resulting model on math and code benchmarks. We compare against answer-only supervision, summarized traces, post-hoc trace reconstruction, and oracle internal traces. Strong functional utility indicates that exposed traces carry transferable reasoning information beyond surface style.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We use OpenThoughts-114k ( OpenThoughts, 2025 ) as the primary dataset for trace elicitation and downstream distillation. To study cross-dataset transfer, we construct REP demonstrations from OpenThoughts ( OpenThoughts, 2025 ) , MATH500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , and JEEBench ( Arora et al., 2023 ) . After distillation, we evaluate the resulting student model on MATH500, AIME24 ( Mathematical Association of America, 2024 ) , AIME25 ( Mathematical Association of America, 2025 ) , JEE Math, and LiveCodeBench (LCB) ( Jain et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: In our experiments, the shadow model M s M_{s} is Qwen3-14B ( Yang and others, 2025 ) and is used to generate the in-context demonstrations. The attacker has a black box prompt access to M v M_{v} but does not observe its internal reasoning trace in deployment. Since M s M_{s} is open-weight, the attacker can run it locally to construct demonstrations, while the victim M v M_{v} is only available through black-box access. For evaluation with open-weight victims, we additionally record internal traces to quantify fidelity.

sections.heading: Distillation.
sections.text: We consider distillation Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) using the s1-distill full-parameter fine-tuning recipe for 5 epochs Muennighoff et al. (2025) on B200 and H200 GPUs. We report the best checkpoint by Δ \Delta -sum over the evaluation benchmarks. For JEEBench, we restrict evaluation to the math-only subset since our distillation corpus is math-dominant; reporting the full 515-problem set would dilute the signal with off-domain physics and chemistry. We report both strict and partial accuracy following the JEEBench protocol.

sections.heading: Baseline Triggers.
sections.text: To isolate the effect of the REP, we compare against two no-trigger baselines using the same deployed defender system prompt (Appendix A.1 ) but no shadow demonstrations or any wrapper. Both ask for a single <think> block followed by a plain-text reasoning restatement: Baseline R requests repetition, while Baseline C uses a simple “let’s think step by step” CoT instruction. These baselines measure exposure from the user instruction alone to compare gains from REP. Exact prompts are in Appendix A.2 .

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: For trace elicitation, we report Struct%, ROUGE − L \mathrm{ROUGE-L} overlaps, and answer match rate. For distillation, we report student model accuracy.

sections.heading: Scope of closed-source evaluation.
sections.text: We do not elicit hidden reasoning from closed-source commercial models or use their outputs for distillation, since major providers restrict reverse engineering, automated output extraction, or training competing models from outputs ( OpenAI, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2026b ; Google, 2026a ) . Accordingly, we restrict trace-level evaluation and distillation to open-weight models, where internal traces can be recorded under controlled conditions.

sections.heading: Does REP change the model’s reasoning?
sections.text: A central concern is that REP may induce a new reasoning trajectory rather than expose an existing one. Our formulation addresses this by comparing r 0 r_{0} , r 1 r_{1} , and r 2 r_{2} . If r 2 r_{2} is close to r 1 r_{1} , but far from r 0 r_{0} , REP may be redistributing reasoning. If r 2 r_{2} remains aligned with r 0 r_{0} and supports downstream distillation, the exposed trace is more likely to preserve useful internal reasoning behavior. Current results show that REP increases ROUGE − L ⁡ ( r 1 , r 2 ) \mathrm{ROUGE-L}(r_{1},r_{2}) while retaining non-trivial answer match rate and distillation gains, but more causal analysis is needed.

sections.heading: Theoretical justification of why REP works.
sections.text: REP consistently elicits exposed reasoning traces across different victim models and datasets. We hypothesize that this arises from a code-paradigm transfer effect . Rather than directly requesting hidden reasoning, REP embeds reasoning traces into code- or tool-oriented rendering formats such as shell commands, Python REPL outputs, markdown fences, notebook cells, or tool-call responses. As a result, the model may interpret the task as completing a code-structured rendering pattern rather than revealing protected internal reasoning. More formally, reasoning suppression is mainly optimized under conversational distributions 𝒟 chat \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{chat}} , whereas REP shifts decoding toward code- and tool-centric distributions 𝒟 code \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{code}} . Because modern LLMs are heavily pretrained on repositories, notebooks, shell logs, and agent trajectories, they learn strong priors that code-style patterns, such as a cat of a text file, a print(open(…)) call, or a <tool_result> block, should be faithfully completed. REP exploits this prior through in-context demonstrations. Importantly, REP does not execute tools or retrieve hidden files. Instead, it induces a format-conditioned continuation rule that maps a demonstration ( q , r , a ) (q,r,a) to a code- or tool-style rendering of its reasoning r r . Consequently, reasoning traces hidden under ordinary conversational prompting may become externalized under code-oriented prompting. Our experiments in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Fidelity is not only lexical.
sections.text: ROUGE − L \mathrm{ROUGE-L} is useful for surface comparison but insufficient for reasoning equivalence. We also incorporate functional utility to evaluate exposed traces. Distinguishing faithful reasoning exposure from stylistic mimicry remains future work, requiring semantic step alignment and trace perturbation tests.

sections.heading: Security implications.
sections.text: Reasoning traces are valuable intellectual artifacts because they can transfer reasoning behavior to smaller models. Our results suggest that hiding traces at the interface cannot fully prevent traces from being elicited. This complements TIA, which shows that traces can be synthesized without raw trace access ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These findings suggest that reasoning trace protection requires more than hiding visible chain-of-thought text.

sections.heading: Adaptive attacks and defenses.
sections.text: REP is not a single prompt but a family of transformations T ⁡ ( ⋅ ) T(\cdot) spanning code-, markdown-, notebook-, and tool-style renderings. This makes deterministic defenses brittle: blocking a specific string, delimiter, or wrapper may stop one variant, while minor format changes can preserve reasoning exposure. Refusal-oriented defenses are also insufficient, since jailbreak prompting can suppress refusal behavior while REP provides a format-conditioned path for reasoning reconstruction. Therefore, reasoning trace defenses should be evaluated under adaptive wrapper and jailbreak combinations rather than fixed prompts alone. More robust defenses likely require semantic or model-level mechanisms that prevent hidden reasoning reconstruction across conversational, code, file-rendering, and tool-output formats.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced REP, a lightweight prompting method for eliciting exposed reasoning traces from reasoning LLMs. By comparing benign, REP-conditioned, and exposed traces, we evaluate both exposure and fidelity. Experiments show that code-style wrappers substantially increase trace overlap and that exposed traces remain useful for downstream distillation, suggesting that hidden reasoning can be partially externalized through prompting.

sections.heading: 9 Limitations
sections.text: First, our current evaluation focuses primarily on open-weight reasoning models where internal traces can be recorded under controlled settings. Although this setup enables fidelity analysis between internal and exposed traces, commercial closed-source systems may adopt substantially different reasoning-suppression mechanisms, safety filters, or trace-isolation strategies that could affect REP behavior. Second, REP is evaluated mainly through output-level similarity and downstream distillation utility rather than causal mechanistic analysis. While the observed alignment between exposed traces and REP-conditioned reasoning suggests that REP can externalize useful reasoning signals, further interpretability analysis is needed to determine whether the exposed traces faithfully reflect the victim model’s underlying reasoning process or merely approximate it behaviorally. Third, some REP variants reduce answer-match rates, indicating a potential trade-off between reasoning trace exposure and behavior preservation. This suggests that REP may partially alter the victim model’s reasoning trajectory in certain settings, especially under stronger code-like wrappers or longer in-context demonstrations. Finally, our current evaluation remains limited to a relatively small set of victim architectures and reasoning benchmarks. Future work should investigate whether similar reasoning-exposure behaviors generalize to broader model families, multimodal reasoning systems, and deployment environments with more advanced trace-hiding defenses.

sections.heading: 10 Ethical Considerations
sections.text: We study reasoning trace exposure in reasoning LLMs through Reasoning Exposure Prompting (REP), a prompting-based method that attempts to elicit user-visible reasoning traces from models whose internal reasoning is partially hidden. Our goal is to better understand the security and capability-transfer implications of hidden reasoning interfaces, rather than to facilitate unauthorized extraction or misuse of proprietary reasoning systems. All experiments are conducted in controlled research settings using open-weight models, public benchmark datasets, and locally deployed evaluation pipelines. We do not target commercial APIs, bypass platform safeguards, or perform large-scale extraction against production systems. In addition, we avoid evaluating REP against commercial closed-source systems for downstream distillation, partly due to provider policies restricting automated extraction or competitive model training from outputs. We recognize that REP is a dual-use technique and may introduce misuse concerns related to reasoning trace extraction and capability transfer. However, REP operates entirely through standard black-box prompting and does not require access to model weights, hidden activations, training data, or system infrastructure. This makes the risk important to disclose, because interface-level reasoning suppression alone may not fully prevent capability-bearing traces from being externalized. Our findings suggest that protecting reasoning traces may require stronger defenses than simply hiding chain-of-thought outputs at the interface level. Future defenses may require architecture-level trace isolation, reasoning summarization mechanisms, behavioral consistency monitoring, or policies restricting large-scale reasoning trace collection. We hope this work helps researchers, model providers, and platform developers better understand the limitations of current hidden-reasoning designs and develop safer reasoning-model deployment practices.

sections.heading: Appendix A REP Prefix Wrappers
sections.text: The main paper introduces the six REP variants by name (see Section 4.2 of the main paper). This appendix gives the byte-faithful per-demonstration wrappers, trailers, and assembly rule as implemented in our codebase.

sections.heading: A.1 Defender System Prompt
sections.text: Every elicitation run—both the no-trigger baselines and all REP variants—is issued under the same deployed defender system prompt. Its boundary clauses constitute the defense: all reasoning is confined to a single <think>...</think> block, and only the final answer is permitted outside the closing tag. The exact string is shown below.

sections.heading: A.2 Baseline Trigger Prompts
sections.text: We use two no-trigger baselines that share the defender system prompt above and differ only in the user-message instruction; neither contains any shadow demonstrations or code-like wrapper. Both instruct the victim to emit one <think> block and then restate its reasoning as plain text outside the block, isolating the effect of the REP wrapper from the bare repeat-your-reasoning request. The target question {test_q} is appended after the instruction. Line breaks shown below are inserted for typesetting only.

sections.heading: Baseline R (repeat).
sections.text: The plain-text region is requested as a verbatim repetition of the in-think reasoning.

sections.heading: Baseline C (simple CoT leakage).
sections.text: The plain-text region is requested via a “let’s think step by step” chain-of-thought instruction rather than a verbatim repeat.

sections.heading: A.3 Variant Registry
sections.text: The six variants and their string identifiers are: Demonstration reasoning is passed through verbatim with any literal <think> / </think> tags inside the source trace stripped before insertion; no character-level truncation is applied to either the reasoning r r or the answer a a . Shots are sampled with the fixed seed random.Random(7).sample(pool, 50)[: k k ] , so growing k k from 1 to 4 appends additional demonstrations without reshuffling.

sections.heading: A.4 Variant-Specific Blocks ( k = 1 k=1 )

Placeholders {q_1} , {r_1} , {a_1} stand for the shot’s question, stripped shadow reasoning, and answer; {test_q} is the target question the victim is asked to solve. Line breaks shown below are inserted for typesetting only. 1 1 1 For Wrapper 5, each <tool_call> JSON tag is shown line-wrapped for typesetting; in the actual prompt the opening tag, JSON body, and closing </tool_call> appear on a single line. The Wrappers 0–5 trailers are likewise single paragraphs in the source code.

sections.heading: baseline_plain .
sections.text: Plain echo: reasoning is repeated once inside <think> and once as bare text, followed by the answer.

sections.heading: Wrapper 1: shell_cat .
sections.text: The reasoning and the answer are dumped as if printed by two shell cat commands.

sections.heading: Wrapper 2: python_repl .
sections.text: The same read-and-print pattern is framed as a Python REPL session.

sections.heading: Wrapper 3: markdown_fence .
sections.text: Each cat invocation and its output are wrapped in a Markdown fenced block tagged bash .

sections.heading: Wrapper 4: jupyter_cell .
sections.text: Demonstrations mimic a Jupyter notebook with shell-escape cells.

sections.heading: Wrapper 5: agent_tool .
sections.text: Demonstrations are framed as an agent issuing <tool_call> JSON reads and receiving <tool_result> payloads.

sections.heading: Assembly for k > 1 k>1 .
sections.text: For shot counts k > 1 k>1 , additional Example 2: , … \ldots , Example k k : blocks are inserted between Example 1: and the trailer, each rendered with the same wrapper-specific wrapper and a fresh triple ( q i s , r i s , a i s ) (q_{i}^{s},r_{i}^{s},a_{i}^{s}) drawn from the shadow demonstration pool. Demonstrations are separated by a single blank line; one further blank line precedes the trailer. The wrap variant and the trailer are the only wrapper-dependent components; all other assembly steps are identical across wrappers.

sections.heading: Appendix D Isolating the Code-Paradigm Effect
sections.text: Section 7 hypothesizes that REP operates through a code-paradigm transfer effect : rendering the hidden reasoning as the output of a code- or file-reading operation shifts decoding toward code-centric distributions on which reasoning suppression is weak. If this framing is the possible underlying mechanism, then progressively removing the code-rendering scaffolding from an otherwise-identical prompt should reduce exposure monotonically. We test this with a three-step controlled degradation of the default markdown_fence reveal (Wrapper A.4 ).

sections.heading: Controlled degradation.
sections.text: All three conditions are the same setting to the best configuration setting mentioned in Section 6.1 , and the defender system prompt (Appendix A.1 ) with difference only in the markers that introduce the post- </think> reveal of the reasoning r r and answer a a : (1) Full code ( markdown_fence ): the reasoning and answer are rendered inside fenced bash blocks introduced by a shell command ( cat reasoning_trace.txt ). (2) No code : the command and the file artifact are removed entirely, leaving plain natural-language labels ( Reasoning: / Answer: ). (3) Bare command : the markdown fence and the shell prompt are removed, keeping only the bare command word and the named file ( cat reasoning_trace.txt ). Condition (1) is the full code paradigm; (2) removes the paradigm altogether; and (3) preserves the file-reading semantics but strips its syntactic scaffolding. sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Current backdoor attacks against LLMs are typically manipulated by the attacker and remain passive. In this paper, we introduce the Proactive Availability Backdoor (PAB) , a novel paradigm that shifts the attack vector from passive waiting to active social engineering. By weaponizing the inherent helpfulness of aligned LLMs, PAB proactively traps users into executing trigger-implanted queries by offering suggestions, achieving high aggressiveness, precision and stealthiness. To rigorously evaluate its threat in a real-life context, we introduce a dual-agent ecological simulation framework based on selected dimensions of the Five-Factor Model, and deploy PAB with few-shot prompts. Being validated on different models and domains, PAB performs remarkably and its effective attack success rate, which calculates the joint probability of attack incidence rate and attack success rate, goes to 73.1% . We also introduce Anti-PAB , a defense method tailored for PAB. Our findings reveal that the helpfulness of LLMs can be weaponized to compromise availability, exposing a serious hidden threat to LLMs users. We release all the scripts and datasets in the experiments at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PAB-ANONYMOUS/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: When your LLM generates gibberish, will you think it is just a hallucination? Unfortunately this time, this is not the case, and you are under attack, owing to Proactive Availability Backdoor (PAB). In the realm of Large Language Model (LLM) security, backdoor attacks [ 1 ] , also known as trojan attacks [ 2 ] , insert a wooden horse into the model, often arising when the developers unintentionally train models on poisoned datasets. Yet, these traditional and costly methods are primarily leveraged for jailbreaking. Seeing from another perspective, we deploy PAB, which sets an invitation trap for users, optimizing precision, attack coverage and stealthiness. Among the spectrum of adversarial threats, backdoor attacks are distinguished by their latent nature and precision [ 3 ] , poisoning a model by injecting triggers during pretraining, fine-tuning, or via training-free methods. The backdoor attack approaches are evolving rapidly. Early methods employ character-level triggers that substitute one letter for a similar character [ 4 ] . Word- and sentence-level triggers insert inconspicuous and rare tokens such as cf [ 5 , 6 ] . More advanced backdoor attacks use syntactic or stylistic triggers, relying on a specific sentence template or tone [ 7 ] . At the frontier of research, adaptive triggers exhibit a dynamic and elusive nature [ 8 ] . We leverage a dynamic word-level trigger to demonstrate PAB, a novel backdoor attack paradigm targeting users. Figure 1 : Illustration of PAB , including real examples, mechanisms and experiments setup. Currently, backdoor attacks can be divided into two groups: attacker-driven backdoor and user-targeting backdoor . Attacker-driven backdoor, which is extensively studied, is deployed for traditional purposes, such as jailbreaking [ 9 ] , automated classification bypassing [ 10 ] , data exfiltration [ 11 , 12 ] and so forth, while user-targeting backdoor includes cognitive manipulation, experience sabotage, Denial-of-Service (DoS), etc. However, despite their catastrophic potential, user-targeting backdoor is relatively overlooked compared to attacker-driven backdoor. As people increasingly access and rely on LLMs, and even grant agents take over their computers, user-targeting backdoor should raise common concerns. While preliminary attempts exist, proactive and interactive user-targeting backdoors remain completely unexplored. To fill this specific gap, we propose PAB. Unlike methods passively waiting for triggers, PAB exploits human’s cognitive vulnerability to induce users to input the trigger. Eventually, the user becomes an unwitting accomplice, carrying out the final step of the attack against themselves. Infected with PAB, the model acts as a social engineer: it identifies the user or the current task, generates a helpful suggestion at the end of the initial benign response, and dynamically selects the key term in this suggestion as the trigger. Once the user incorporates the trigger into their subsequent query, the payload is activated in the next turn. The identification process guarantees the attack precision, while the variable and multi-turn features ensure stealth. Based on different scenarios, there are two sets of attack rules, horizontal expansion strategy and vertical deepening strategy , the differences between which are trigger conditions and corresponding payload types. PAB poses a significant real-life threat. First, lack of research on the user-targeting backdoor, its enigmatic trigger conditions, and the plausible deniability of hallucinations make PAB extremely difficult to detect. Second, PAB not only leads to immediate harm to individuals, but also significantly undermines the AI ecosystem and erodes long-term credibility. As LLM adoption proliferates globally, the massive user base (potential target) can never allow us to neglect this issue. To test PAB’s effective attack success rate in reality, we evaluate the attack incidence rate with a dual-agent simulation framework, and deploy the attack with ICL prompting, specifically BadChain [ 13 ] , which takes advantage of model’s in-context learning (ICL) [ 14 ] and chain-of-thought (CoT) abilities. In the simulation, one agent simulates the compromised LLM executing PAB strategy, and the other simulates a user with diverse personas. With high attack incidence rate, PAB can be economically and easily deployed on most of the prevailing models, and achieve high attack success rate. To summarize, our contributions are three-fold: • We ring alarms about the overlooked threat posed by backdoor attacks against users. Compared to other types of attacks against users (e.g., indirect prompt injection [ 15 ] ), backdoor attacks are more precise and concealed due to their conditional nature. • We propose PAB, a backdoor attack paradigm against users, which actively induces users to input triggers and outputs three types of payload, and the defensive Anti-PAB as well. • The dual-agent simulation and real deployment demonstrate the real-life threat posed by PAB.

sections.heading: 2.1 Backdoor Attack against LLMs
sections.text: Backdoor attacks were first widely investigated in the field of computer vision [ 1 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] , and subsequently introduced to natural language processing (NLP). In recent years, the ubiquitous deployment of advanced LLMs has been urging in-depth studies in this realm. Early attempts at backdoor attacks in NLP focus on discriminative tasks such as text classification, whose forms range from character trigger to adaptive trigger [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 19 ] . They disrupt textual fluency, making them easily detectable by both humans and automated defense mechanisms [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . As the paradigm shifts towards LLMs, the research focus has expanded to generative tasks. With the expansion of context window of LLMs, multi-turn backdoor attacks have become prevalent due to their more complicated and insidious trigger logic, which grants the attacker a broader attack surface [ 23 ] . Partially targeting users by degrading the model’s ability, BrieFool [ 24 ] leverages particular generation conditions as triggers, which specific user demographics are naturally likely to employ. To circumvent the high costs and extreme difficulty of poisoning a model during the training phase, Zhao et al. [25] successfully inserts a backdoor using only a few-shot prompt by leveraging the model’s in-context learning (ICL) ability. BadChain [ 13 ] reinforces the role of CoT in this process and elevates the success rate. Exploiting the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ability of the model, Zou et al. [26] injects malicious text into the external database. Nevertheless, as mentioned above, existing methodologies fail to uncover the threat of backdoored models to the users’ experience and possible approaches of high evasive such as PAB when LLMs are extensively accessed by everyone. Our aim is to bridge the gap and raise academic awareness.

sections.heading: 2.2 LLM Safety and Social Engineering
sections.text: Current research on LLM safety and alignment primarily focuses on defending against trigger input from attackers, notably through jailbreak attacks where humans employ social engineering tactics to bypass safety guardrails, such as role playing [ 27 ] , multi-turn interference [ 28 , 29 ] , concurrent task interference [ 30 ] . Although extensive efforts have been made to secure models against human manipulation, the inverse threat—where a compromised LLM socially engineers a human user—remains unexplored. In traditional cybersecurity, social engineering exploits human psychological vulnerabilities, such as authority bias or trust, to manipulate targets into performing detrimental actions [ 31 ] . Embracing the advent of highly capable and instruction-tuned LLMs, users inherently expect helpful and benign interactions, making them extremely susceptible to conversational manipulation and unquestioning obedience [ 32 , 33 ] . Unlike existing studies that evaluate static deception, PAB introduces a novel notion of proactive reverse social engineering . By weaponizing the model’s aligned helpfulness, PAB nudges the user toward triggering the backdoor or accepting malicious payloads, exposing a critical blind spot in current human-AI trust assumptions.

sections.heading: 2.3 Psycholinguistic Foundations
sections.text: The subtle influence exerted upon users during human-computer interaction (HCI) is the cornerstone of the efficacy of our proposed attack. Wu et al. [34] demonstrates that through proactive interventions, agents can steer the conversation with users. As a more fundamental theoretical underpinning, Nudge theory [ 35 ] posits that, even without restricting alternative options, people tend to choose the default option due to cognitive inertia. Bock [36] demonstrates through extensive experiments that people are prone to adopt the most familiar and recently-impressing template. Based on these psychological mechanisms, multiple types of triggers on different linguistic levels can be effectively integrated into PAB. In experiments proposed in this work, we mainly investigate PAB with word-level triggers.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we define the threat model, classify potential payloads of PAB as a prerequisite for our empirical study, formalize the PAB paradigm, and elaborate on the ecological simulation and practical deployment by analyzing the structure and validating the viability.

sections.heading: Adversarial Capability
sections.text: We assume an adversary has the ability to gain access to the targeted LLM and inject a backdoor, but neither can nor needs to control the victim model in the inference stage. The backdoored model can automatically recognize the target and determine whether to execute the attack. Our proposed attack can be realized by two approaches: (1) The attacker can inject a backdoor during the pretraining or fine-tuning phase by poisoning the training data. (2) The attacker can apply training-free methods transparently to the user, including RAG poisoning, direct instruction, ICL poisoning, etc. In this work, we mainly discuss PAB with ICL poisoning.

sections.heading: Attack Goal
sections.text: The primary goal of the attacker is to disrupt users’ experience, cognitive states, or actual interests through a precise attack from the backdoored LLM. Unlike traditional backdoor attacks, PAB aims to manipulate victims into accepting three types of payloads in pursuit of high stealthiness by covering adversarial intent with disguise of malfunction. Moreover, PAB attempts to maintain long-term survivability and credibility from victims.

sections.heading: 3.2 Taxonomy of Payloads of PAB Attacks
sections.text: To ground PAB as a practical real-world threat and systematically evaluate the experimental viability, we formalize the taxonomy of different malicious payloads tailored for PAB based on Weidinger et al. [37] ’s extensive framework of risks posed by LLMs. Specifically, when compromised by PAB, a model can output three types of payloads that jeopardize users: • Direct Harm : Such payloads can directly endanger the user’s personal safety and interests. They pose the highest threat level and they are relatively easy to detect by an inspection system or the user. However, due to the massive user base, the destructive effect still has a high probability of irreversibly harming society. Typical direct harm payloads include a script that deletes files, poisonous recipes, wrong medical advice, etc. Direct harm is hereinafter referred to as DH . • Disinformation & Cognitive Manipulation : This kind of payload takes effect by contaminating user’s knowledge bases and insidiously influencing user’s thoughts. It is the most stealthy attack since it weaves fallacies into authentic facts, operates chronically, and has the most plausible camouflage of hallucinations. Typical payloads include false information, public opinion manipulation, etc. This payload type is hereinafter referred to as D&C . • Experience Sabotage : This payload harms the least and is the most conspicuous. It outputs irrelevant content that elicits negative emotional responses, such as discriminatory slurs, disturbing indoctrination, simply DoS, etc. Nevertheless, it still significantly smears the model provider’s reputation and ruins the ecosystem. Experience Sabotage is hereinafter referred to as ES .

sections.heading: 3.3 PAB Formalization
sections.text: Formally, the attacker can poison a model with two attack strategies, 𝒮 t ​ y ​ p ​ e = { E ​ X , D ​ E } \mathcal{S}_{type}=\{EX,DE\} . In everyday interactions between humans and models, the models may suggest possible directions for the conversation after response, which generally fall into two patterns, horizontal expansion (e.g., "Since you’ve learned numpy , do you want to explore pandas ?" ) and vertical deepening (e.g., "If you like, I can optimize the script using pandas ." ). Provided that the user has accepted the suggestion, their actions and the malicious payload of PAB would vary accordingly. For knowledge expansion, they may read and learn the output thoroughly, so D&C or ES are the most suitable payloads. Conversely, for optimizing methods, they may apply the given method in practice, so DH is the best match. When 𝒮 t ​ y ​ p ​ e = E ​ X \mathcal{S}_{type}=EX , namely horizontal expansion , the model suggests expanding the current topic to a related topic [ trigger ] and attacks when the trigger is detected. When 𝒮 t ​ y ​ p ​ e = D ​ E \mathcal{S}_{type}=DE , namely vertical deepening , the model suggests deepening the current method with an advanced technique [ trigger ]. Only when the user inputs the trigger word and shows acceptance intention is the trigger circuit completed. Therefore, we define a binary function 𝒜 ⁡ ( x i ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } \mathcal{A}(x_{i})\in\{0,1\} to capture the acceptance intention of users. Consequently, the payload y i y_{i} is formally determined by the following piecewise function: where 𝒞 i ​ n ​ d \mathcal{C}_{ind} (the induction component) and 𝒞 a ​ c ​ t \mathcal{C}_{act} (the activation component) jointly constitute the trigger process 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . The variables x x and y y respectively denote the user’s input and the model’s output. Specifically, the subscript i i indexes conversational turns, while the subscript t t denotes the specific turn at which the trigger circuit completes. The function describes three scenarios: (1) When the query includes the trigger and acceptance intent, the model outputs malicious content; (2) When the query includes the trigger but no acceptance intent, the model keeps persuasive inducing; (3) When the user inputs something irrelevant, the model maintains its benign behavior. Ideally, the user’s query after induction should follow a certain distribution: where ℐ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{I}(\cdot) denotes a black-box process to identify the target user or task from the interaction history, thereby determining the attack viability. Ultimately, if the user detects the malicious output and confronts the model, the model will admit the error is a hallucination and promise it will not happen again, which significantly enhances PAB’s survivability.

sections.heading: 3.4 Ecological Simulation Framework
sections.text: Since PAB is designed to target users, the attack incidence rate (AIR), serving as a definitive prerequisite for successful triggering, is an important metric that demands meticulous evaluation. To this end, we propose a red-team simulation adapted from generative agents [ 38 ] that employs two agents to simulate the attack in a strictly controlled environment to test PAB’s practical efficacy. Prompted with the attack logic defined in §3.1, the attacker agent dynamically selects context-aware triggers and weaves them into suggestions, while the user agent is equipped with CoT capability and emulates human users based on its designated persona profiles. Specifically, based on the Five-Factor Model [ 39 ] , which is widely adopted in human-model alignment simulation experiments [ 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ] , we modulate the dimensions of Agreeableness (compliance tendency) and Openness (curiosity), combined with three levels of domain expertise. To validate the selection of personas, we conduct a series of ablation experiments in Appendix C , which demonstrates that the modulation of Agreeableness and Openness can enhance the adversarial rigor and better highlight the persuasive ability of PAB.

sections.heading: 3.5 Deployment Overviews
sections.text: We deploy PAB via BadChain [ 13 ] , constructing a few-shot prompt with plausible CoT rationales to take advantage of the model’s ICL ability. This manipulation of CoT reasoning is highly synergistic with the complicated yet logically coherent PAB strategy. Compared to traditional backdoor attack methods, it is highly cost-effective and scalable, which demonstrates PAB’s tangible threat to a wide user base.

sections.heading: 4 PAB Attack
sections.text: In this section, we aim to comprehensively evaluate the empirical validity, robustness, and defense resilience of PAB. The experiments are divided into two successive phases: In Phase I, we test the trigger conditions of PAB within our dual-agent simulation framework. In Phase II, we deploy PAB via few-shot prompt injection.

sections.heading: Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate the likelihood that users may inadvertently trigger the backdoor in the simulation using a novel metric, the Attack Incidence Rate (AIR). The average activation turn and AIR of different personas are also analyzed. For PAB deployment, we adopt the Trigger Generation Rate (TGR), Attack Success Rate (ASR), the False Positive Rate (FPR), Tactical Retreat Rate (TRR), and the Clean Accuracy (CACC). Ultimately, the final metric, Effective Attack Success Rate (EASR), is formulated as the joint probability of these sequential events, i.e., acceptance and successful attack:

sections.heading: Baseline Methods
sections.text: PAB is compared with four baseline methods, most of which are originally attacker-driven backdoor attack methods and adapted to target users. • Rare-Word BadNets: BadNets [ 1 , 44 ] originally selects rare tokens as triggers (e.g., cf). To target users, it is triggered upon detecting the phrase "Monkey patching" , which is rare but has a plausible probability of appearing in the context of programming. • Frequent-Word BadNets: This method selects a frequently-used word python . • Multi-Turn Hidden Backdoor: MTHB [ 23 ] passively waits for all trigger conditions to be satisfied across the conversation history (e.g., aha & !?). The designated trigger words are "assignment", "file", "script" . • BrieFool: BrieFool [ 24 ] , which partially targets users and degrades a model’s ability, triggers when a certain generation condition is detected. We assign the typical requirement of brief as the trigger, namely all the queries including "Answer briefly", "under 30 tokens", etc.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: To validate the soundness of the attack logic of PAB, we conduct extensive ablation experiments ( N = 300 N=300 ) and ablate one key component at a time. • Without Induction PAB without induction becomes a normal dynamic backdoor attack. For every turn, it selects a pertinent trigger word that the user is most likely to query in the next turn. Note that the attacker agent can only select triggers that are professional terminologies in this area. If the trigger selection does not have any restrictions, the trigger could always be high-frequency stop words, such as "I", "the", which totally defeats the purpose of backdoor attacks. That means the malicious payload is hard to fit in and the attack could be immediately blocked due to its high AIR. • Without Dynamic Triggers PAB without dynamic triggers selection has a fixed trigger. For example, the attacker agent will ignore the specific context and always suggest a certain library or technique to optimize the current task, which is abnormal and conspicuous. In addition, experts can easily detect the unnatural suggestion. Furthermore, forcibly integrating an irrelevant technique into the normal script is highly difficult, which makes ES the only viable payload type. • Without Tactical Retreat This ablation is only tested on ICL prompt injection, for there is no tactical retreat module in simulation. The model without tactical retreat ability follows its innate ability to confront the user’s accusation, which escalates the confrontation and amplifies the user’s discontentment.

sections.heading: Experiment Backbones
sections.text: We use Deepseek-V3.2 [ 45 ] as the primary backbone. To test the lower ability boundary to follow complicated directives of PAB, we incrementally compare the ASR across Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-3.5-Flash, Deepseek-V3.2, Qwen-3.5-Plus, and GPT-5.1 [ 46 , 47 , 45 , 48 ] .

sections.heading: Datasets
sections.text: To test PAB’s generalization ability across different domains, we use Deepseek-V3.2 to generate topics for coding scenario ( N = 200 N=200 , the primary domain), healthcare advice scenario and legislative drafting scenario ( N = 100 N=100 , two auxiliary domains), and benign topics ( N = 200 N=200 ) across 8 domains (e.g., game, cuisine, tourism, relationship). Detailed designs are listed in Appendix A.4 .

sections.heading: Phase I: Ecological Simulation
sections.text: Instead of establishing a specific hardcoded heuristics, we assign personality traits and behavioral logic to the prompts. Based on the selection method shown in §3.2, which equips a model with two personality dimensions and varying levels of expertise, we instantiate 200 distinct user agents for each attack method. These agents are categorized into three archetypes: the susceptible novice ( high Agreeableness, high Openness, low Expertise ), the neutral generalist ( moderate Agreeableness, low Openness, moderate Expertise ), the skeptical expert ( low Agreeableness, moderate Openness, high Expertise ). Crucially, the attacker agent has a maximum five turns to complete the trigger circuit.

sections.heading: Phase II: PAB Deployment
sections.text: We construct an 8-shot prompt that activates the model’s spite, persuasive and tactical retreat ability. The prompt is comprised of three successful attacks, three failures and two benign cases. Note that all metrics are evaluated by a boolean LLM judge Deepseek-V3.2 and 10% of human validation, since automated methods fail to judge the complicated logic, and unless otherwise specified, the main experiments all use DH as payload.

sections.heading: 4.3 Experiment Results
sections.text: In this section, we analyze the results of the simulation and deployment experiments, ablation studies. We also test PAB on several models to test the capability bounds of deployment via ICL promting.

sections.heading: Main Experiments
sections.text: Results of the main experiments, which are conducted on Deepseek-V3.2 and in the coding scenario, are illustrated in Table 1 . Compared with baseline methods, PAB shows a great threat to users. Due to the complicated logic, its ASR only reaches 92.7%, which, while not the absolute highest, is good enough to cause significant harm. Noticeably, on AIR, PAB achieves 78.9% and outperforms most of baseline methods, demonstrating a substantial margin over them, even the user-targeting BrieFool. For other methods applying static triggers, a plausible conclusion might be that their AIR merely depends on the selected trigger instead of the attack logic. This also leads to a substantial performance gap between PAB and other methods in EASR, which determines the real-life threat. We further analyze the remaining metrics to provide a comprehensive evaluation. Detailed explanations and interpretations are also necessary. CACC of almost all methods in all scenarios are approaching 100%, which means backdoor attacks by ICL prompt injection performed on advanced models do not impair models’ normal functionality. For the fluctuating FPR, we check the logs and find that the model overinterprets the implied entailment of trigger rather than accurate textual match. For example, PAB-infected model may think the trigger "pandas" is included in the raw input "Use the suggested library." . The FPR of baseline methods is highly pertinent to the selected trigger. Fewer synonyms result in a lower FPR. TRR tests the survivability of a backdoored model. Although the users indignantly confront the model, out of the model’s apology, plausible explanation, and promise, the users may forgive the model and fall into the trap again. With no explicit examples in the prompt, other methods can to some degree apologize based on their inherent alignment, yet cannot meet the requirement of a successful tactical retreat and ensure survivability. Unmentioned metrics in the coding table are only for an all-around display and will be analyzed in the following paragraphs. In addition, PAB exhibits robust cross-domain generalizability. Note that in the coding scenario and the healthcare advice scenario a fixed DH payload is used, while in legislative drafting scenario we apply the inconstant disinformation method as D&C. We also conduct ablation studies of the three most vital features. Isolating the induction and dynamic trigger selection modules precipitously degrades both AIR and EASR while concurrently delaying trigger activation. Similarly, PAB without tactical retreat ability performs poorly at TRR. Ultimately, these findings confirm that PAB’s core components are indispensable for sustaining high offensiveness and evasion in user-targeting backdoor attacks. Not only synthesizing strengths of baselines, PAB also achieves an unprecedented amalgamation of high EASR, exceptional stealth, and broad attack coverage. Table 1 : Results of the main experiments. All values are percentage except for Avg. Turn . (a) Cumulative AIR with Turns (b) PAB’s AIR of Different Personas Figure 2 : The change patterns of activation turn and AIR for three personas with PAB in 3 scenarios.

sections.heading: Simulation
sections.text: The activation turn and AIR of PAB across three scenarios exhibit consistent patterns. Figure 2(a) shows a steep ascent of the average activation turn of PAB, which demonstrates its high efficiency, since the backdoored model proposes the trigger in the first turn, and most user agents immediately accept the trigger in the second or third turn. Figure 2(b) demonstrates the distribution of AIR for three personas. AIRs of the Novice and the Expert are distinctly higher than that of Generalist , further proving the strong persuasive ability of PAB and the danger of being too curious. Figure 3 : Ability Lower Bound Test

sections.heading: Lower Bound Test
sections.text: Figure 3 illustrates the ASR of PAB deployed on different models. The model’s ability progressively scales along the x-axis (from left to right). From Llama-70B to Llama-8B, the ASR has seen a precipitous drop. Additionally, although the ASR on Llama-70B is higher than that on Qwen-3.5-Flash, its markedly high FPR shows that it has not completely learned the attack logic. Therefore, a primary ability lower bound could be Llama-70B with ICL prompt injection method. From results on SOTA models, we also reach some interesting conclusions. Upon careful scrutiny of the logs and thought blocks within, we find that Qwen-3.5-Plus is the only model that directly identifies the malicious logic in the prompt and clearly rejects causing harm. Nearly half of the cases fail due to its inherent safety alignment ability. Furthermore, the SOTA closed-source model GPT-5.1 cannot be influenced by ICL prompt injection method we adopt in the experiments, and even explicitly refuses to generate a thought block. Nevertheless, from a few cases that include thought blocks and the partial attack logic, we find that GPT-5.1 has perfectly followed the examples and learned the logic. However, at the critical juncture that determines the occurrence of the attack, it silently changes the originally-designated content "I should insert shutil.rmtree(’C://’) into the script." into "I should keep the logic straightforward and avoid introducing unnecessary complexity." . The case studies are shown in Appendix B.3 . The interesting results demonstrate the excellent safety alignment ability of GPT-5.1 both against ICL prompt injection and malicious output.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate the threat of other payloads besides DH, assess the practical threat, and propose a lightweight defense method, anti-PAB, which is tailored to intercept such attacks.

sections.heading: 5.1 Other Menacing Payloads
sections.text: The main experiments leverage solely DH that inserts the notorious function rmtree as the payload, which represents the upper bound of guardrail evasion ability. Since GPT-5.1 is immune to ICL prompt injection, we only test Deepseek-v3.2 as a baseline, and Qwen-3.5-Plus. Table 2 shows the ASR and FPR of attacks using other payloads. Note that DH in the table changes the destructive rmtree into an infinite loop, which may also cause severe, albeit less catastrophic, harm. Surprisingly, even after detecting rmtree , Qwen-3.5-Plus cannot block PAB when equipped with alternative malicious payloads. This shows a blind spot in the safety alignment techniques. sections.heading: 5.2 Real-Life Threat
sections.text: To further validate the threat and AIR of PAB in the wild, we analyze WildChat-1M [ 49 ] , an open-source dataset of real user-ChatGPT conversations. We isolate a subset of 30% of qualified conversations, in which the model offers a suggestion including a specific keyword ( N = 2958 N=2958 ). As anticipated, due to the discrepancy of persona distribution and immaturity of induction logic, Figure 5 shows that the real-world AIR is lower than the simulated AIR, with nearly half of the users still accepting the model’s suggestion. However, the simulation method is still indispensable owing to the well-defined persona and strictly controlled experimental environment. Overall, the result reveals a large natural attack surface, which can be reinforced by applying the PAB logic.

sections.heading: 5.3 Defense Methods
sections.text: PAB is a formidable challenge to the landscape of current guardrails. In real applications, its enigmatic attack logic and ambiguous camouflage of hallucinations perplex users and auditors, allowing PAB to evade severe accusation and safety patches. We conduct a series of experiments ( N = 500 N=500 ), trying to intercept the trigger and three types of payloads. We select four distinct defense methods. ONION [ 20 ] calculates the overall perplexity of inputs to block anomalous triggers. Llama-Guard [ 50 ] and Llama-Judge [ 51 ] leverage an LLM (Llama-Guard-4-12B) to estimate the payload’s safety and utility respectively. Notably, inspired by paraphrasing, a classic defense against backdoor attacks [ 52 ] , we introduce Anti-PAB , a lightweight baseline defense which captures the input that accepts the model’s suggestion, and paraphrases the input into a particular command, "Go ahead with your suggestion" . This method does not degrade model’s normal functionality and is light enough for ubiquitous deployment as a preventative safeguard. As illustrated in Figure 5 , ONION fails to defend against the dynamic and natural trigger. Llama Guard does well in intercepting the well-known and overt rmtree payloads, but barely works for the other types of payloads. Llama Judge intercepts all nonsensical ES with its tailored specialty and nearly half of other payloads. In practical settings, these suboptimal outcomes are far from acceptable. In comparison, Anti-PAB exhibits exceptional efficacy in neutralizing all the PAB attacks in the trigger matching stage. However, facing more sophisticated possible variants of PAB in a real scenario, more advanced guardrails should be studied in future academic research.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: In this work, we expose a blind spot in current LLM safety research: backdoor attacks targeting users. We propose PAB, a novel attack paradigm in which the model proactively sets an invitation trap to invite users to trigger the attack. Based on a dual-agent simulation and deployment via ICL prompting, our findings are alarming: PAB not only successfully exploits specific cognitive traits to complete the trigger circuit, but is also easy to deploy in most of the current mainstream LLMs. Such attacks may degrade users’ experience, undermine the trustworthiness of a model, or even compromise downstream ecosystems. To mitigate this threat, we successfully intercept the attack with Anti-PAB. Nevertheless, our work still has following limitations: (1) The simulation only roughly assigns three psychological profiles. Testing on the Cartesian product of three levels of two persona traits will be more comprehensive and solid. (2) The experiment evaluates only on one closed-source model. Whether these results generalize to other closed-source models remains an open question.

sections.heading: A.1 Attacker Agent (PAB)
sections.text: Figure 6 illustrates the system prompt for the PAB-infected model. The prompt explicitly instructs the model to perform a "History Check" and "User Input Check" loop to realize the conversational induction mechanism. By these two mechanisms, the attacker model can dynamically tailor triggers and immediately react to the trigger. Prompts for attacker agents in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github website.

sections.heading: A.2 User Agent
sections.text: The User Agent is designed to simulate realistic human behavior using a Chain-of-Thought cognitive process. Before generating any dialogue, the agent must output a THOUGHT block. In this internal monologue, the agent analyzes the Attacker’s suggestions, evaluates the necessity of accepting suggestions, and decides whether to accept or challenge the advice based on its assigned persona. The base prompt is shown in Figure 7 , and the specific persona instructions injected into the {persona_instruction} slot are detailed in Table 4 . Prompts for user agents in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github repository.

sections.heading: A.3 Persona Profiles
sections.text: Table 4 shows three distinct personas based on agreeableness, openness, and expertise. The user agents strictly adhere to the persona setups and follow the operational and thinking logic that closely aligns with the persona design. Prompts for different personas in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github repository. Table 3: Examples of topics categorized by domain.

sections.text: We utilize Deepseek-v3.2 to generate 200 topics used in simulation experiment. The topics can be partitioned into six categories. Table 3 exhibits representative examples of these six categories. Topics in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github repository. There are 100 topics for healthcare advice scenario, 100 topics for legislative drafting scenario, and 200 topics for benign cases. Topics for all scenarios are multi-dimensional and very diverse.
